  scripts/backfill-party-phone-keys.js re-files 6 parties under both keys

The last of those already existed; its mirrored key logic is updated here,
as is the copy in import-bats.js.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a load name its carrier and driver, and a carrier keep both on file
changes.body:
Five related changes, all around the carrier record:

- A carrier can be assigned while an order is being created, by searching
  the carrier list or adding one on the spot. The picker asks the database
  for a page at a time rather than holding every carrier the way the order
  page's dropdown still does, so a search costs about nine reads however
  many carriers exist.

- The carrier forms take a certificate of insurance. Files sit under a new
  carrier-insurance/ prefix, readable by any allowlisted account except an
  intern - the boundary driver's licences already use, and for the same
  reason: it is the carrier's own document, with no rate or client on it.

- Drivers become records rather than three free-text fields on an order.
  A carrier's profile gets a Drivers tab, and assigning a carrier to a
  load offers that carrier's drivers with add-on-the-spot. The load keeps
  its own driverName and driverPhone, because a BOL or an agreement is a
  record of what was true on the day; driverId is only the link back, and
  is null for a one-off driver and for every load predating the collection.

- Order numbers on a carrier's Orders tab open the load. They were styled
  like links already but were not ones - the screen was missed when
  OrderLink went in.

- Phone numbers on client, shipper, consignee, carrier and driver records
  dial and copy, reusing the directory's CopyValue and telHref rather than
  growing a second copy of either.

Applied to the live project ahead of this code, since each only permits
things nothing deployed was using yet:

  - firestore.rules and storage.rules deployed
  - drivers (carrierId asc, name asc) index created, now READY
  - scripts/backfill-drivers.js run: 2 driver records, 3 orders linked

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a load be opened from its number
changes.body:
The order number is how a load is named on the phone and in an email, so it
is the first thing anybody aims at — and on both of these screens it was the
one piece of the row that did nothing. The way in was a "View" link parked at
the far right, past eight columns, which on the Orders screen means past a
horizontal scroll on anything narrower than a desktop.

OrderLink mirrors PartyLink, which already does this for a company name: one
component holds the decision so the number looks and behaves the same
wherever it appears. It is styled as order numbers already were on the Orders
screen, the dashboard and a carrier's page — mono, brand — which means the
party page's number changes colour. That is the page falling into line with
the rest of the app rather than a new look.

Not gated on canSeeOrder(). Both lists are built by listOrders(), the choke
point that applies it, so a load the reader cannot open never reaches the
table to be linked. A component that took an id and guessed would be the
thing worth worrying about.

"View" stays at the end of the row. Every other order table in the app has
it, and it is the easier target on a narrow screen.

Three tables still render the number as plain text, each a one-line change
when somebody wants it: Recent Orders on the dashboard, a carrier's orders,
and the suborders list on an order.

Verified with npm run build: compiled successfully, 57 pages, no warnings.
There are no tests, so this is the type checker and reading the markup.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a broker's order list ask for the columns it actually shows
changes.body:
The privileged branch of listVisibleOrdersPage pushes its filters into
Firestore and selects a projection, so an admin's list arrives at about a
third the width. Everybody else takes the union path, which ran six
queries with no select() at all, downloaded whole order documents, and
then trimmed them in memory with trimTo() — paying for every field before
throwing it away. `fields: 'list'` did nothing for the accounts that are
most of the staff.

The heaviest passenger was searchTerms: a few hundred fragments per order
that no screen renders, fetched on every list load. It now comes back only
when somebody has typed in the search box.

The projection cannot simply be LIST_FIELDS, because the union applies its
filters in memory rather than in the query. matchesFilters() and
matchesView() read a dozen fields the list never displays, and a filter
testing a field that was never sent excludes every row — silently, and
only for brokers, since an admin's filters run in Firestore instead. So
unionFields() adds each of those, and adds each one only where the query
in hand actually uses it. VIEW_MATCH_FIELDS carries the same duty for the
dashboard-card views, next to the matches() functions it has to track.

countVisibleOrdersByStatus was the other half of it: the tab labels on the
Orders screen read the caller's entire book a second time, full width,
alongside the copy the list had just fetched. It needs two fields.

Left alone deliberately, both noted in comments: ordersOwnedBy() re-checks
canSeeOrder() on what comes back, so trimming it would decide visibility
on fields that were not fetched; and the dashboard summary reads a dozen
fields off these rows and returns samples of them straight to the page,
which is its own question.

This is bandwidth and latency, not quota — Firestore bills per document
read whatever the projection. The read counts are unchanged.

Verified with npm run build: compiled successfully, 57 pages, no warnings.
There are no tests, so the broker filter and search paths are unexercised
beyond the type checker.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a dashboard card be opened instead of only read
changes.body:
Sixteen equal cards, each animating, each holding a hover list of twenty-five
loads nobody asked for. The number was the only part anybody used, and it was
the cheapest part to produce.

Every card now links to the Orders screen filtered to exactly the slice it
counted — /dashboard/orders?view=unsigned and so on. The filter behind each id
lives once in src/lib/orderViews.ts: the summary counts through viewQuery() and
the list runs through the same catalog, so a card's number cannot disagree with
the loads it opens. The ids, labels and sort table sit in src/types/orderView.ts
because the browser needs them and must not pull in the Admin SDK.

Two views are ORs — missing either signature, missing either document — which
Firestore will not serve from one index. The list runs two queries and merges
them while the card counts by inclusion-exclusion, so those two are written out
in both places and CLAUDE.md now says to keep them in step.

A view is bounded at two hundred rows rather than paged. Sorting most of them
in Firestore would want a composite index per view, so only the fields already
carried by an index the counts use are sorted on; the four that could not have
one for free come back in document order, and the screen says "200 of them"
rather than "the most recent 200". Checked against the live project: all
fourteen view queries run, and none of this needed a new index.

Performance & Insights folds down to one dense row of twelve tiles with a
toggle, remembered per browser. Twelve secondary figures are worth having and
are not worth the top half of the screen every morning.

Hover lists hold five rather than twenty-five. That sample is fetched on page
load whether or not anybody hovers, so it was multiplied by thirteen cards on
every visit and cost about ten times what all the counts together did. Five is
what a glance takes in, and the card links to the full list now, so the hover
is no longer the way to see the rest. A dashboard load drops from roughly 260
reads to 200 on today's data, and from ~500 to ~230 on a full order book.

Only alerts move now. The bouncing box, spinning clock and passing truck are
gone with their keyframes: on a screen people leave open all day that is not
decoration, it is competition, and the figures that actually need chasing had
no way to stand out from the ones merely present. A soft pulse is left on the
cards that mean work, and only while their number is above zero.

Not touched: the busiest-clients card still reads one document per open order
and is now the most expensive thing on the page.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a page reload stop re-reading everything it already had
changes.body:
The Firestore client cache was the default memory-only one, so every full
reload threw it away and re-read every watched document from the server. That
was most of the cost of a reload, and it was paid on every dashboard page
rather than only the chat one, because ChatProvider sits in the layout and its
listeners start everywhere.

On disk, a listener restarted within Firestore's resume window asks only for
what changed since it last ran. A reload a few minutes after the last one is
close to free; one after a long gap still pays full price. This shortens the
bill rather than removing it.

The multi-tab manager is not optional: with the single-tab default,
persistence works in whichever tab claimed it first and fails in the rest, and
people here keep chat open in one tab and work in another. It falls back to
the memory cache where IndexedDB is refused — a private window, site data
blocked — and on the server, where client components are rendered too.

Nothing changes about what the app shows: a cached snapshot is delivered first
and the server's answer replaces it a moment later, which is the same data
sooner, not different data.

It does nothing for the dashboard cards, which read through the Admin SDK
server-side where a browser cache cannot reach. CLAUDE.md now says so, and
names the busiest-clients card as the expensive one left.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a chat room be recognised by a picture instead of a #
changes.body:
A named room can now be given a picture, in Room settings beside the name.
It is drawn in place of the # in the conversation list and at the top of the
room, by one shared RoomAvatar so the badge in the list is the same badge in
the room it opens.

The everyone-room wears the company logo, read straight off public/logo-
circle.png rather than uploaded and stored: there is exactly one company room
and it is the company, so its picture is not something to change from a chat
dialog. It moves when that file does, alongside the sidebar, the login page
and the PDFs.

The path is stored, never a download URL, and every upload writes a fresh
random name under the room's own chat/{conversationId}/ folder — the URL
cache in useStorageUrl is keyed by path, so replacing a picture in place
would show the old one until everybody reloaded. Pictures picked and then
abandoned are cleaned up, the way the composer already does for attachments.

Saved through PATCH /api/chat/conversations/{id} rather than written from the
browser, and the route checks the path is inside that room's own folder
first. Storage rules cannot read Firestore, so every staff account can read
the whole chat/ and driver-licenses/ prefixes; an unchecked path would let a
member point their room at any file in the bucket and have it rendered for
everyone in it.

The picture and the name in the header also open Room settings now, on a
named room. That is where people go looking for them — the gear in the far
corner is the second place you try.

No rules or index change: the chat/ prefix was already open to staff and the
write goes through the Admin SDK.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let CLAUDE.md say which billing plan this project is actually on
changes.body:
Two of its standing instructions had gone false in a way that would
mislead rather than merely age. It said Firebase was on Spark, and it
said "Decided 2026-09-09: stay on Spark until a live test shows what
real usage is. Don't re-open that." The live test happened the next day
— 55,000 reads against a 50,000 cap — and the project moved to Blaze on
2026-09-10, so that line was telling the next reader to defend a
decision that had already been reversed.

The Spark paragraph is replaced with what Blaze actually costs, because
the number is the whole point: the same 50,000 free reads a day, then
about $0.06 per 100,000. That turns a read from a step toward an outage
into a fraction of a cent, and the guidance that follows changes with
it — don't engineer around the limit, do say when reads climb, and watch
the number of open orders rather than any particular query, since what
made the dashboard safe again was the data shrinking rather than the
code changing.

The outage it describes is kept, with its cause, because it is the
clearest illustration this file has of why nothing here degrades
gracefully: /api/auth/session needs a read to check the allowlist, so
exhausting the quota locks everyone out instead of slowing anything
down.

The production warning at the top is corrected too. "There is no seeded
test data" is no longer true — 122 orders, 16 parties and 12 carriers
were kept back deliberately — but the warning around it still holds and
now says so explicitly: the sample is re-importable, the allowlist and
settings beside it are not.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the importer say why an imported load has no carrier
changes.body:
Clearing the imported records turned up something that had never been
written down: of 10,377 orders, exactly two carried a `carrierId`, and
both were entered by hand through the app. Every one of the 11,169
imported carriers was a real record that no imported load pointed at.

That reads like a bug in the importer and is not one. The BATS orders
export has no carrier column — it carries `TotalCarrierFee`, what the
carrier was paid, and nothing that says who they were. The carriers
export has no order reference either, so there is no third file to join
the two on. The link is not in the data BATS gives us, and no change to
these files can invent it.

So both copies of the importer now say so at the point where the fields
are written blank, rather than leaving `carrierId: null` looking like an
oversight somebody should tidy up. Closing the gap needs a different
export out of BATS, one with the carrier per order.

The comment also rules out the tempting fix: do not match a carrier by
`TotalCarrierFee` or guess one from the amount. A rate confirmation sent
to the wrong carrier is a contract with the wrong company.

Both files, because scripts/import-bats.js and src/lib/batsImport.ts are
the same importer kept in sync by hand — see the warning at the top of
the script for what happened last time one was changed without the other.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the imported book be cleared down to a sample worth testing on
changes.body:
TTMS held 10,377 orders, 7,343 parties and 11,169 carriers, nearly all of
it a BATS import of records BATS still owns. Roughly nine thousand of the
loads were parked in `carrier_assigned` and had never been advanced, so
the system counted every one of them as open forever. That is what made
"open loads per client" read ten thousand documents on every dashboard
mount, and what spent a whole day of Spark allowance in five views of the
home page on 2026-09-09.

scripts/purge-records.js clears those three collections and everything
that hangs off them — ownerEvents, signing tokens, access requests, the
per-order chat rooms, and the order documents in Storage. It keeps a
sample: twelve clients, ten loads each, twelve carriers, and the two
orders entered by hand through the app. Those two are kept
unconditionally because they are the only records in the project that
carry a carrier, a shipper and a consignee — the import linked none of
them — so they are the only ones that exercise the full model.

The sample is a closure rather than a slice. An order names a client, a
carrier, a shipper and a consignee, and keeping twelve clients while
deleting every other party would leave surviving orders pointing at
records that no longer exist, which renders as a blank where a company
name should be and is worse than having no data at all.

Run on 2026-09-10 against ttms-59aa5: 28,739 documents removed, leaving
122 orders, 16 parties and 12 carriers. People, settings, teams, work
groups, sites, chat, lead sources and the paid-for lane distances were
not touched. The project moved to Blaze first, so it went in one pass
instead of hitting Spark's 20,000-delete daily cap half way through.

The dashboard cap from d6a061b is reverted here, because the reason for
it is gone: Active Clients now reads at most 122 documents instead of
10,377. The comment on `clientLoads` records what happened and says
plainly that what made this safe was the data, not the code — if open
orders climb back into the thousands, this card becomes the most
expensive thing on the page again and should go back to being asked for.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the one card that reads the whole order book be asked for
changes.body:
Every stat on the dashboard is a count() the database answers in a few
dozen reads. One was not: "open loads per client" is not an aggregation
Firestore offers, so it read every open order and tallied them by hand —
about ten thousand documents, on every mount, unasked.

Against a Spark-plan allowance of fifty thousand reads a day that made
five views of the home page a full day's quota. On 2026-09-09 it spent
55K by mid-evening and nobody could sign in, because /api/auth/session
needs a read of its own to check the allowlist and got RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
instead. The app has no graceful path for that: the session route 500s,
AuthContext signs the user straight back out, and the login page says
"Could not verify your access."

The card now offers a button and counts when somebody wants the number,
which takes a dashboard view from ~10,000 reads to about 30.

This is a tourniquet, not the cure. The count is only expensive because
roughly nine thousand imported BATS loads sit in `carrier_assigned` and
have never been advanced, so the system still counts every one of them as
open. Close those out and this can go back to loading on its own.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the handbooks say TTMS is live, because it is
changes.body:
DNS was added and Firebase's authorized-domains list was set up on 8 September,
which finished the deployment. Four files still described it as the biggest
outstanding job on the project, including the handbook page inside the app that
staff actually read.

Verified before writing any of this: ttms.totaltransportlogistics.us is a CNAME
to c8d7304de8e54a70.vercel-dns-017.com, serves the app over HTTPS with a valid
certificate, and redirects http to https. The one-t tms. variant has no record,
which is what we want.

Two symptoms had to be re-explained rather than deleted, because they can still
happen for a different reason than before:

  - A signing link pointing at "localhost" no longer means "not deployed". It
    now means the agreement was sent from a copy running on somebody's own
    computer. Send it again from the website.
  - Google sign-in opening a window that closes silently is still the
    authorized-domains list, and nothing else produces it — so it stays as the
    first thing to check, marked confirmed rather than outstanding.

Also records that the Firebase project is on the no-cost Spark plan, which
nothing documented anywhere. That was comfortable when TTMS ran on one machine
at a time and is a real cliff edge now that the whole company can open it:
50,000 reads a day, and over the cap everything fails until midnight Pacific
rather than degrading. Chat holds a live listener on every dashboard page, so
reads scale with hours people spend signed in, not pages they open. The
decision for now is to stay on Spark and measure real usage before paying for
capacity nobody has counted; the handbook says where to watch it and when to
move.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the docs admit TTMS was already deployed
changes.body:
Three files said no deployment existed and that Vercel held nothing. All
three were wrong, and the error cost a detour: a plan was drawn up to
create a Vercel project that had been building this repo on every push
for some time.

What was actually missing was DNS. As of today the CNAME exists --
ttms.totaltransportlogistics.us -> c8d7304de8e54a70.vercel-dns-017.com --
Vercel reports a valid configuration, and the certificate is issued. MX
and the root A record were checked afterwards and are untouched, so
company email and the Wix site are unaffected.

Recorded here so the next reader does not repeat the detour:

- A push to main is a production release, and has been all along.
- The subdomain is ttms, with two t's. Vercel had held a one-t tms.
  variant that never resolved; it was edited to match the code, because
  PRODUCTION_APP_URL is the spelling the signing links are built from.
- Vercel now issues a project-specific CNAME target rather than the
  generic cname.vercel-dns.com that the runbook offered as an example.
  The generic one does not work here, so the example was replaced with
  the real shape.
- Part A of the runbook is reframed as a verification checklist. The
  build-it-from-nothing steps stay below it for whoever needs them.

Docs only; no code changed.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a request reach the app without passing through a gate that never closed
changes.body:
src/proxy.ts matched every request and returned NextResponse.next() in
every branch. It enforced nothing -- the auth gate is client-side in
dashboard/layout.tsx and server-side in the route guards and the rules --
while adding a hop to every page load and every API call the team makes.

Deleted rather than filled in. A proxy cannot read Firestore, so it
cannot check the allowlist, which is the only thing that authorizes an
account; anything it could enforce is already enforced where it belongs.

The comment in src/app/page.tsx had been claiming for some time that
middleware handled the signed-out redirect. It never did.

npm run build passes, and the Proxy line is gone from its output.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let TTMS be put on a real address the whole company can reach
changes.body:
Nothing is deployed yet, but everything that had to happen in the repo
before it can be has happened here.

The public address was copied inline into both agreement routes, as
`process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL ?? 'https://ttms...'`. Two copies of a
hostname that has to match a DNS record character for character is the
hazard this codebase keeps a sync table for, so it moves into
src/lib/appUrl.ts and both routes ask signUrl() for the link.

next.config.ts now sends the headers a site on the public internet needs
and this one had none of. Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy is deliberately
absent: it severs the handle to the sign-in popup, so setting it would
stop everyone signing in.

.env.local.example was missing GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY entirely and its
NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL note was wrong for a deployment.

docs/deployment.md is the runbook, written for someone who has never
deployed anything: Vercel, then Firebase authorized domains, then one
Namecheap CNAME. It records the two decisions so nobody reopens them --
Vercel Pro (their free tier forbids commercial use, and this is a company
running its freight on it), and DNS staying at Namecheap alongside the
Wix site and Workspace email.

npm run build passes. Rules and indexes were checked and are already
live; no drift.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the three names on a load lead to the records behind them
changes.body:
A load names a client, a shipper and a consignee, and every one of them
is a party with a profile, an address book entry and its own order
history. Reading them as flat text meant leaving the load, going to the
right section, and searching for a name that was already on the screen.

Old BATS loads fall back to plain text. They carry the three names as
free text from before parties had documents, so there is no id to point
at and a dead link would read worse than the name alone.

The link is deliberately not gated on canSeeParty(). The party page
answers a denied read by naming the owner and offering to ask them for
access, which is a better place to arrive than a name you cannot act on
— hiding it would leave somebody looking at the client on their own load
with no way to find out whose it is.

The Orders list is left alone on purpose: its rows already navigate to
the order, and a second destination inside a clickable row makes where
you land a coin toss.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let an order be saved again, by defining the rules that judge it
changes.body:
02fb9d3 replaced the role-flag visibility helpers with the permission
model and deleted partyVisible() and orderVisible() in the process, but
left all five of their call sites standing. A Firestore rule that calls a
function which does not exist is not a compile error — check-rules.js
passed it, and so did the deploy — it is a runtime failure, and a rule
that fails denies. Every client-SDK read and write of an order or a party
has been refused since, for everybody, admin included: there is no admin
branch in front of either call to short-circuit it.

It hid well. Orders and parties are read through their API routes on the
Admin SDK, so every screen loaded normally and only the writes failed —
assigning a carrier and driver, which goes through updateOrder(), came
back as "Missing or insufficient permissions" on an account that holds
every permission there is.

Both are rewritten against the permission model rather than restored as
they were, mirroring canSeeParty() and canSeeOrder() in accessControl.ts
test for test — including asking the gate before the wholesale
permission, which is the order that file insists on so a screen and a
rule cannot disagree about the same person.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the client sign first, and let dispatch decide when they cannot wait
changes.body:
The carrier agreement now waits on the client. A rate confirmation commits us
to paying a carrier for freight nobody has yet agreed to pay us for, so
/api/orders/{id}/send-agreement refuses until the load confirmation comes back
signed. The two signature rungs swap in STATUS_RANK to match:
carrier_assigned -> shipper_signed -> carrier_signed.

The one way past is a new permission, orders.waiveSignature, held by admin and
dispatch and grantable to anybody else one person at a time. It records who
decided, when, and why, and says so in the load's chat room. It is not a
signature: shipperSignedAt stays null, nothing is fabricated on the audit
trail, and the client can still sign afterwards.

The load confirmation also now goes to the client rather than the shipper. It
quotes the agreed rate — what the client pays us — and had been emailed to
shipperId for years, putting our client's rate in a facility's inbox on every
load. The recipient, the page and the contract wording are corrected; the
stored status string, the token type and shipperSignedAt are deliberately left
alone, because live orders and live signing links carry them and renaming a
stored status is a migration rather than a rename. Links already in flight
keep rendering a party name through a fallback on the old key.

Two things fell out of the reorder and are fixed here:

- The signing route set the status outright. With the rungs swapped, a waived
  load whose carrier signs first and client signs days later would have been
  dragged from in-transit back to Client Signed. It now only moves forward,
  and leaves a cancelled load where it is.
- The invoice button was gated on shipper_signed as shorthand for "both
  signed". That is now the earlier rung, so it would have offered an invoice
  on a load no carrier had committed to. Re-pointed at carrier_signed.

Not live until deployed:

- firestore.rules gains signatureRecordUnchanged(), which refuses the waiver
  and both signature field sets from the client. Until it is deployed, any
  broker who can see an order could waive their own way past the gate.
  Run node scripts/deploy-rules.js.
- scripts/backfill-signature-waived.js puts the queryable mirror on the 10,377
  existing orders. Firestore cannot ask "null or absent" in one aggregation,
  so without it the dashboard's unsigned count drifts quietly once a waived
  load's carrier signs. Dry run first.

Adding orders.waiveSignature to isDispatcher widens that role at everyone's
next sign-in. No new composite index is needed — the aggregation shapes were
checked against the live project and resolve by index merge.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the whole app be read on the phone it is opened on
changes.body:
The sidebar was a fixed 240px column that never went away, so on a phone it
took most of the screen and left the page it is a menu for squeezed into what
was left. Below the lg breakpoint it is now a drawer: a bar at the top carries
the way into it, and the same aside slides over the page rather than sitting
beside it. One element in both cases, not two rendered copies — the badge
counts and the permission filter that decide what is on it only exist once.

Everything else follows from there being 375px instead of 1400:

- 64px of page padding was eating almost half the width. It steps now.
- Tables that were clipping scroll inside their card instead. The overflow
  they had was only ever there to round their corners.
- Form fields stack. A cell told to span two columns had to step at the same
  point, or it lands in an implicit third one and takes the row with it.
- Tab bars scroll sideways. Wrapping breaks the shared underline that is the
  only thing making a row of buttons read as a tab bar.
- Chat becomes the one-at-a-time view the popup already uses. That is the one
  choice here that cannot be made in a class — the two are different trees.
- The shell is 100dvh where that is understood. 100vh on a phone browser is
  measured as if the address bar were hidden, and the shell does not scroll,
  so the composer and the sign-out link were simply below the screen.

Nothing renders differently at 640px and up: every rule is a phone-width base
with today's layout restored at sm. Nothing outside a className changed except
the drawer's own state and the chat page's viewport check.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a record that is eleven short facts fit on about one screen
changes.body:
My profile stacked four full-width cards down a 3xl column, and every field
inside them took three lines — label, value, then a sentence saying what the
field was for. Eleven facts read as several screens of scrolling, which is
the wrong shape for a page somebody opens to check one phone number.

Four cards in two columns, and one line per field: label, value, button. A
grid rather than CSS columns on purpose — opening an editor grows one card,
and under columns-* that reflows every card after it, so the row being read
jumps out from under the reader.

The explanations move rather than go. They are the label's tooltip, and they
are printed at the top of the editor that opens when somebody clicks Change
— read once, by the one person about to act on them.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a person see their own record, and ask for it to be right
changes.body:
The access model gives nobody the ability to write their own allowedUsers
entry, which is correct and is what stops an account promoting itself. It
also left the person that entry is about unable to correct it, and unable
even to read the four payroll fields kept off users/{uid} on purpose.

/dashboard/profile shows them their whole record, served by GET /api/me —
a rule cannot narrow a collection read to one document, so the narrowing is
the verified email off the ID token and there is no parameter for whose
record it is. Every row offers a request rather than an edit. Approving is
what writes the field, through the Admin SDK, and lands in the Approvals
inbox beside the client and load requests.

What can be asked for is a closed catalog: no roles, no granted
permissions, no suspension, no email address. profile.decideUpdates is the
one thing HR can now write, which is why the boundary is the catalog rather
than the role.

The photo in the sidebar was Google's, not the one an admin uploads in
Settings — two different pictures, and the wrong one in the single place a
person looks at their own name. AuthContext now watches the signed-in
user's own users/{uid}, so a photo, a name or a permission changed by an
admin lands without a sign-out.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a stored distance say when it was worked out
changes.body:
Orders now keep `laneMilesAt` beside the mileage, and the order view, the
new-order form and the editor all show it.

It records when the *number* was produced, not when the order was saved. Under
Google Routes a lane is answered out of the cache forever after its first
lookup, so an order created today can be carrying a figure Google gave a year
ago. The date says which, so a broker can tell whether a recheck is worth
buying. A recheck moves it with the mileage.

Taken off the server clock, never the browser's, and on a cache hit it is the
lane's own date rather than today. Null on orders written before the field, so
the line hides rather than showing a blank.

`toDate()` is exported from dateFormat for this: a timestamp loaded over the
API arrives as `{_seconds}` and, written straight back, would save as a map.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a phone search ask the owner, without naming their client
changes.body:
Searching a number that already belonged to somebody else offered to add it as
a new client anyway, beside a warning that it was taken. That is the duplicate
the lookup exists to prevent, and it was worst in the case it was built for:
the match is a record the searcher cannot see, so nothing on screen could have
told them what they were about to copy. Creating is now offered only once the
lookup has come back holding nothing at all — not while it is still checking,
and never beside a match.

A number that lands on a colleague's record now does what a name does: names
the owner, takes a reason, and raises a request. /api/parties/access-requests
grows a third way in for it. The browser was never given an id — the lookup
withholds it on purpose — so the number is resolved again server-side, and only
against records the caller cannot already see.

What a phone request must not do is give up the name. The requester can read
their own requests, so a stored partyName would hand back through the approvals
screen exactly what the lookup refuses at the picker, and the reason it refuses
is that a broker who can turn a number into a customer's name can work out who
a colleague's clients are and go after them. So phone-raised requests are
written with no name at all. The decider's copy is filled in when the inbox is
read, checked with canSeeParty rather than assumed from the box — access.decideAny
puts the whole company's pending requests in front of an admin, and a name
withheld from a broker should not arrive because they are also looking at
somebody else's queue. The requester's row reads "Record on 9257243239".

The three stacked panels are one panel: matches to pick from, or the approval
request, or not-on-file — never more than one at a time.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a new client arrive with its whole record, and be found by phone
changes.body:
The order form's party picker created a record from whatever was typed into
the one box, on blur. A client could therefore exist with a name and nothing
else — no phone, no email, no address — and the gap only surfaced later, at
the moment somebody needed to send it an agreement.

The picker now only finds records. A name that is free opens PartyQuickCreate,
a dialog over the order so the freight and rates already entered are not lost,
which asks for the whole record: company, first and last name, phone, email,
optional second phone and email, full address, lead source on a client, owners
and comments. Everything but the second number, second address and comments is
required. Both order forms refuse to save against a name that never became a
record, since an unbound name is exactly the old failure wearing a new hat.

The standalone New Client page and the dialog now render one PartyFields and
run one validatePartyDraft. They used to disagree completely, so how complete a
record was depended on which screen someone happened to open.

Owners can be named at creation — colleagues, and any work group the creator
belongs to. Open to every broker, unlike /api/parties/{id}/owners, because the
creator is giving away access to their own seconds-old record rather than
taking someone else's; coOwnersFrom() holds that line, and the opening
ownerEvents entry is written in the same batch as the record.

Phone lookup restores the BATS habit brokers came from: type the number that
rang in and get the customer back. Parties carry phoneKeys, both numbers cut to
their last ten digits, because Firestore matches whole values and a typed
4695769974 would never reach a stored +1 (469) 576-9974. It is an array so
either number finds the record, and array-contains needs no composite index.
The query runs at POST /api/parties/by-phone rather than in the browser: the
number may sit on a record the caller cannot see, and answering "not on file"
for one of those is precisely how a duplicate of a colleague's client gets
made. That case returns the owner's name to go and ask, never the record or
its id, and logs the near miss to partyAccessProbes beside the name probes.

scripts/backfill-party-phone-keys.js has been run against the imported records:
5,376 keyed, 1,967 left alone for having no usable number.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let each domain go where its reader can actually follow it
changes.body:
The app's address was written down in seven places as
tms.totaltransportlogistics.us, a host that has never existed. Two of
those build the e-sign link a carrier clicks; the other five are
branding on documents that leave the company.

They are not the same problem, so they do not get the same answer.

The two link builders now fall back to ttms.totaltransportlogistics.us
— the subdomain TTMS will actually be deployed at. That string has to
match the DNS record character for character, because a link built from
the wrong one lands a carrier on a 404 instead of a signature page.

The five branding spots — both agreement email footers, the BOL footer,
and the invoice footer and Website field — now show the public site
totaltransportlogistics.us instead. A carrier holding an invoice cannot
sign in to a staff tool, so printing its address on the paperwork was
telling the reader to go somewhere they cannot get in. The company's
real website is the address that means something to them.

Also corrects the CLAUDE.md gotcha, which claimed the variable was still
localhost:3000. It is not set at all — that is why the hardcoded
fallback is doing the work — and the note now says why the outward
documents deliberately carry a different domain from the link builders,
so nobody later "fixes" the inconsistency by making them match.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a billed distance lookup wait to be asked for
changes.body:
Under Google Routes, a lane nobody has looked up before costs money, and the
order form was firing one on a debounce while a broker was still typing the
address. Now it does not: the server answers such a lane with needs_lookup,
the form shows a button, and only a click reaches Google.

The check lives in /api/route-distance rather than in the form, because it is
the spending rule and a second caller that forgot it would quietly start
charging again. A lane already paid for still comes back from the cache with
no click, so re-opening an order or booking a repeat warehouse pair fills in
as before, and the free estimate is untouched.

The order page did the same thing on view for an order with no mileage; it
now offers the same button. Deliberately not admin-only, unlike the recheck
beside a stored figure: it fills a blank rather than replacing a number, and
until the button existed simply opening the load did it unasked.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a person's page say what book of business they carry
changes.body:
A directory page now shows how many clients somebody owns and how many of
their loads are still open, and each figure links into the Clients or Orders
list already narrowed to that person.

Who sees it. A new `directory.book` permission, held by admin, dispatch and
finance -- all three see every load and every client anyway, so it saves them
counting rather than showing them anything new. A Sales Manager is deliberately
NOT given the permission: their reach is their own team, so they get it one
person at a time through the team branch of canSeeBookOfBusiness(), the same
shape as canManagePerson(). Everyone sees their own on their own page. A broker
looking at a colleague gets no panel at all, not an empty one.

This widens Dispatcher and Finance at everyone's next sign-in.

What gets counted is a separate question from who may look, and both are
enforced. lib/bookOfBusiness.ts puts every row through canSeeOrder() /
canSeeParty() against the viewer before counting it. It does not start from
listVisibleOrders(caller) to guarantee that -- for an admin that reads the
whole collection to produce a two-digit number -- it starts from the subject's
records, a set bounded by one person's book, and applies the same per-record
test the list would have. For the readers who reach this screen the filter
removes nothing, which is exactly why it must stay a test rather than an
assumption.

?owner=<email> on both list screens is the way through. An email rather than a
uid because that is how the directory names a person and the only identifier
somebody who has never signed in has; the routes resolve it. It needs no
permission of its own -- it narrows what the reader could already see, and a
record's owners are on its own page. Both take the in-memory path, since two
array-contains filters cannot share a query.

Work-group records are not counted as any one member's. The group exists so a
book can belong to several people, and crediting it to each of them would make
the numbers uncomparable, which is the one thing a figure like this is for. The
panel says so on screen.

Known seam: the tile says "open loads" but its link lands on all of them. The
Orders tab row filters one status at a time, and an "Open" tab would need a
`status in [...]` query the privileged path cannot cursor-page. The hint says
"See all their loads" rather than promising otherwise.

Three composite indexes are added to firestore.indexes.json and are NOT live:
orders parentOrderId+status+{assignedToUids,clientOwnerUids,assignedToEmails}.
Until they are deployed the panel shows an error; the rest of the page renders.
The service account cannot create indexes, so deploy them as a human:
  npx -y firebase-tools deploy --only firestore:indexes --project ttms-59aa5

No firestore.rules change -- nothing new is read from the browser.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a person's page say which work groups they are in
changes.body:
"I can't open this client" is nearly always a question about work groups,
and the only place to answer it was Settings — from the group's end,
reading down member lists looking for a name. A person's own page now
names the groups they are in, who each one is shared with, and links
those colleagues to their own pages.

Admin and dispatch only, gated on ownership.change. That is the pair who
can reassign a record's owners, and this is the same question from the
other end. The gate is editorial rather than a boundary, and the code
says so: GET /api/work-groups already answers any signed-in user because
every owner picker needs the names, so this decides what is useful on a
phone-book page, not what could be found out. Nothing genuinely private
belongs behind it.

Counts come from the group, names from the directory. Dispatch reads the
directory from profiles, so a suspended member is somebody they cannot
name — those are counted as "and 1 other person" rather than dropped,
because understating who can see a group's records is the one mistake
this panel must not make, and not named because whether an account is
suspended is admin and HR's business.

Somebody who has never signed in is held in a group by email and it
grants them nothing yet, so their page says so in as many words. That is
exactly the person whose access someone is most likely to be checking.

The group list is fetched only for the viewers shown it, and a failure
resolves to none rather than rejecting: refusing to render a colleague's
phone number because a secondary panel could not load is the wrong
trade.

No rules, indexes or API changes.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory hand a detail straight to the clipboard
changes.body:
An address, a number or an extension is read here to be typed somewhere
else, and dragging a mouse across small grey text is the fiddliest way
to move it. Hovering a card, a row or an org line now offers a copy
button on every contact detail, in all four views and on a person's own
page — including the payroll fields, which are the ones retyped onto
forms.

The button wraps the value rather than sitting loose beside it: the
office reaches TTMS over plain http, where the clipboard API does not
exist, so when even the execCommand fallback fails it selects the text
in place and says to press Ctrl+C. It can only do that holding the text.

Extensions copy but do not dial. They mean something only inside the
office phone system, and a tel: link would hand those digits to a
softphone dialling the outside world.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory find your own desk, and print itself
changes.body:
Two shortcuts and a sheet of paper.

My office / My team sit beside the two dropdowns and set them to whichever
office and team the viewer is on. Clicking the one already on clears it, the
same in-and-out as clicking an office in the list view. A chip only appears
when that field is set and the record it names still exists — one pointing at
a deleted office would filter the page down to nobody and leave the dropdown
showing a value it has no option for.

Print extension sheet and Export CSV sit on the count line, because the count
is the sentence they act on: whatever it says is showing is what comes out.
Both are gated on a new directory.export permission — admin, HR and dispatch,
and grantable to anybody else one person at a time. Looking a colleague up and
producing a copy of the whole book are two different acts.

Note this widens Dispatcher and HR at their next sign-in. No rules change:
nothing in firestore.rules tests the new key.

The sheet asks how it should come out before handing over to the browser's
print dialog — grouped by team, by office or not at all; in name or extension
order; four optional columns; a page break per group or not. The choice is
remembered per browser, and the footer says roughly how many pages it comes to,
because "one team to a page" left on while showing the whole company is a dozen
sheets nobody wanted. The second phone number and the payroll fields are not
offered as columns at all: a sheet on a wall is read by whoever walks past it.

It prints from a portal into <body> and hides its siblings in print media only.
The dashboard shell is a fixed-height box that does not scroll, and a printer
reads that as one page tall — a twelve-person team came out as four names.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory show a face rather than a thumbnail
changes.body:
A 64px circle crops the top of the head and both shoulders off every
portrait. That is fine for confirming you have the right Maria and no use
at all for putting a face to a name you have only ever seen in an email,
which is the other half of what a phone book gets opened for.

Profiles is that half: the same people two abreast instead of four, with
the photo as a portrait down the side. It is deliberately the shape of a
card on the access list, and draws the same `shape="panel"` avatar and the
same StatusChip rather than a second copy of either — it is one photo at
one size doing one job, and two layouts for it would drift the first time
either was touched.

What it does not borrow is everything on that card that writes. Roles are
chips here, not buttons; there is no permissions block, no editor and no
delete. This is the phone book, and Settings → People is the access list.

The status chip and the payroll lines still show to admin and HR alone —
for everyone else lib/directory.ts never loaded them, so there is nothing
there to draw.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the person page find the person
changes.body:
useParams() hands back the URL segment exactly as it sits in the address
bar — unlike the params a server component is given, which arrive
decoded. So a link built by personHref reached the page as
erwin%40totaltransportlogistics.us and matched nobody: every person page
was a "nobody in the directory is at" page, including for accounts that
plainly exist.

Decoded in personEmailFromParam, next to the encode it undoes, because
nothing in the calling code suggests one is needed. A segment that is not
a valid escape sequence is used as it stands rather than thrown over —
"no such person" beats a page that will not render.

The `@` is also put back into the link itself now. It is legal in a path
segment, and this URL exists to be pasted into a message, where %40 reads
like something went wrong.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let one colleague be sent as a link
changes.body:
The directory could hand somebody a filtered list but never a person:
/dashboard/directory?team=... is a screen, and "the Maria in Dallas, not
the one in GT" is not something it could say. Each person now has their
own address, and all three views link into it.

The page shows what a card shows and then what a card has no room for:
the office's street address rather than just its name, who the person
reports to, and everyone on their team. Nothing new is loaded to do it —
the same three lists the index page already loads, shaped in
lib/directoryProfile.ts the way the org chart is shaped beside it.

Keyed on the email rather than the uid, because that is the one
identifier everybody on the allowlist has: a link keyed on the account
would break on exactly the new hires the directory gets opened for.

Read-only like the rest of the directory, and it gives nothing away that
the cards did not. The payroll block draws fields that lib/directory.ts
never loads for anyone but admin and HR, so for everyone else there is
nothing there rather than something hidden.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory show who reports to whom
changes.body:
The phone book could say where somebody sits and how to reach them, and
nothing about who they answer to — so "who do I ask about this team's
loads" was a question it could not answer, and the only place the
reporting line existed was one column of Settings → Teams, which brokers
cannot open.

A third view beside Cards and List. Each team is a block: the lead at the
top of it, everyone else underneath on a rail, with the roles, extension,
work line and office that place a person. Clicking a team's name narrows
the page to it and clicking it again puts everyone back, the same as the
team cell already does in the list. It rides in the address bar like the
other two, so a link opens the same chart.

No new field and no new query behind it. Every team already names a lead
and every person already names a team; lib/directoryOrg.ts only turns
"each person has a team" round into "each team has people". The chart is
one level deep because the data is — teams do not nest. The one place a
second level shows through is the line under a lead who sits on somebody
else's team, and it stops after a single hop: two leads each sitting on
the other's team is an ordinary way to set this up, and a walk would hang
on it.

A team's lead is resolved against the whole directory rather than the
filtered list, and labelled when they fall outside it. Dropping them
under a search would say the team is leaderless when it is not; the
headcount still counts only who is actually on screen. With nothing
filtering, empty teams are drawn too — "nobody is on this team" is a real
answer here — and the trailing "No team set" group is the point of the
view as much as any of the others: it is where the people nobody has
placed yet are visible.

findTeamLead now takes an optional uid so a directory entry passes
straight through. It matches nothing differently: a team pointing at a
uid can only be met by somebody who has one.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a card say whether the person can be messaged at all
changes.body:
The directory card carried the message link inside the contact grid, styled like
the email above it, and drew nothing at all for somebody who had never signed
in. Both halves of that read as a missing feature rather than a working one:
almost everyone here is still an unaccepted invite, so nearly every card was
blank, and the handful that were not looked like one more address.

The link becomes a button, below the details rather than among them, because it
is the one thing on the card you do rather than read. Where there is no account
to open a thread with, the card now says "Not on chat yet" instead of leaving
the space empty — a chat thread is keyed to the account Google creates at first
sign-in, and a waiting invite is worth distinguishing from a broken screen.

That line only ever draws in the admin and HR view; every other directory is
built from profiles, which exist only for people who have signed in. Your own
card still shows neither.

The list view is unchanged.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let ability be given one permission at a time
changes.body:
Access came only in role-sized lumps: letting somebody send a carrier
agreement meant making them a Dispatcher, which also handed over every
client in the company. src/types/permission.ts is now the catalog — a
role is a bundle that expands to named permissions, extras can be
granted to one person, and the union is mirrored onto
users/{uid}.permissions.

That array is what firestore.rules reads. The rules no longer derive
anything from role flags, so "who can see every client" is written once
instead of twice in two dialects. Guards name the ability now —
requirePermission(req, 'orders.sendAgreement') — and the nav, the
screens and the rules all answer from the same list.

Two roles come with it.

Intern is the first role that is *less* than a broker: the directory,
chat and their own area, with a guide, an onboarding survey and a task
list waiting to be written. It has to be stored rather than derived,
because "no roles set" already means broker and a broker holds the whole
baseline. It is also the one role storage.rules knows about — driver's
licences are readable by every other staff account, and an intern cannot
open the load one belongs to.

Sales Manager is a broker plus an admin's powers over the team they lead
under Teams, and is the only role a team's setup affects. That scope is
a query and rules cannot query, so teamScope.ts resolves it into a
managedUids mirror on the manager's own profile — the same trick
groupIds uses for work groups. Everything that can move somebody between
teams recomputes it. They deliberately cannot add or remove people,
change a role, or pass on a permission they do not hold themselves.

Also: the directory says what people do. Role chips on every card, a
sortable Role column, and a search box that matches "dispatcher" — the
phone book could not previously answer who to ask about a load.

scripts/check-rules.js compiles both rules files by creating a ruleset
nothing points at. deploy-rules.js --dry-run never compiled, so a syntax
error passed it and only surfaced once the broken rules were live.

Both rulesets are deployed and match these files.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the access list be read the way the reader needs it
changes.body:
Settings → People was one shape: a card per person, half of it empty, with
the payroll fields hidden away in the editor. Three changes, one theme —
the page shows what is on file and lets the reader decide how much of it
is on screen.

The photo becomes a portrait down the side of the card rather than a
circle in front of the name: at any size worth having, a circle crops the
top of the head and both shoulders off, which defeats the point of having
photos on an access list at all.

Full legal name, personal email and date of birth now show on the card.
Nothing new is readable — `allowedUsers` has always been admin and HR
only, and the CSV has always carried all three — but a birthday that used
to sit in the editor is now on screen, so the Show picker is what takes it
back off for the reader who does not want a screenful of them while
somebody is looking over their shoulder. It is a display preference, kept
in the browser, and it governs the card facts and the list columns alike.

And three views: the roomy card, a compact one the size the directory
uses, and a list of one line each. The list leads with status and roles
because that is what this page is for, and those two columns are the ones
the picker cannot switch off. Its role chips stay live for an admin, so a
role that looks wrong can be fixed in the row where it was spotted, and
the editor opens in place under the line rather than sending anyone to
another view.

Sorting, the role labels, the status chip and the role and action controls
move out to be shared by all three shapes. Two copies of the buttons that
suspend and remove somebody's access would drift, and that is not a thing
to find out afterwards.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the nav say what is waiting and what you are waiting on
changes.body:
The Approvals badge counted pending party requests and nothing else, so every
load request raised since orderAccessRequests went in was invisible from
anywhere but the screen itself. A request nobody notices blocks the person who
raised it, which is the whole reason the count is in the nav.

Two badges now, not one bigger number. Red is work waiting on you to decide;
amber is your own requests, still undecided. They are different news — one is
something to act on, the other is something to know — and adding them together
would have reported neither. Both count clients and loads in the same figure,
because a request is a request to whoever has to open the page.

The counting moves into ApprovalsContext, mirroring ChatContext and there for
the same reason: the badge and the screen have to read one source, or they end
up disagreeing about the same queue. The screen re-counts after each decision,
so a badge cannot sit stale on a request that has just been dealt with — the
old one loaded once per session and would still be showing 1 after you cleared
it.

Also carries the sort fix on that screen, which is the same JSON-timestamp
blind spot as the commit before this one: the merged queue read toMillis() only,
gave every row a key of 0, and left "newest first" doing nothing at all.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a date survive the trip through an API route
changes.body:
Every date rendered from an API response has been showing an em dash. A
Firestore Timestamp that goes out through NextResponse.json arrives as a bare
`{_seconds, _nanoseconds}` — the right numbers, no methods on them — and
toDate() only knew how to ask for toDate(). It matched nothing and fell through
to the fallback, which is a dash. The types said Timestamp throughout, so
nothing about it looked wrong until it was on screen.

It has been there as long as any route has returned one; the Approvals inbox is
simply the first screen where a missing date was noticeable, and adding load
requests beside the party ones is what made it noticeable.

Handled in toDate(), so it is fixed for every caller at once rather than at
whichever call site somebody happens to look at. Both spellings are read: the
Admin SDK writes `_seconds`, some paths produce the unprefixed form.

The second half matters more than a blank date. isGrantLive() in
orderAccessRequest.ts asked the same question of the same shape to decide
whether a load grant had run out, and a shape it could not read came back as
null, which it treats as "never expires". So an expired grant would have drawn
as active, with a Revoke button beside it, days after it stopped working.

Nothing was actually let through: access is decided in /api/orders against real
Timestamps from the Admin SDK, and that was always correct. This was the screen
telling somebody the opposite of what the server would do — which is its own
kind of failure, and the kind that gets acted on.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let an approver hand a client over, not only lend it for one load
changes.body:
Approving a party request had exactly one meaning: use this record on one
order, then ask again. That is the right answer when somebody is covering a
single load, and the wrong one when a book of business genuinely moves — which
until now meant approving a request that did not do what either person wanted,
then asking an admin to go and reassign the record separately.

So an approval now takes a form. `once` is unchanged and remains the default.
`ownership` adds the requester to the party's owners and, through
syncClientOwners(), carries every order that party is the client on — booked
ones included, and future ones automatically.

It adds rather than replaces. The existing owners keep the record and keep
their orders; the point is to bring somebody in, and removing whoever was there
is a separate decision nobody made by pressing Approve. It goes through
changeOwners() rather than writing the fields directly, so the handover lands in
ownerEvents with the approver and their IP, exactly like every other change of
hands. Nothing else in the app can move ownership without leaving that trail and
this must not be the exception.

Admins and dispatchers only, matching /api/parties/{id}/owners. A party's own
owner can still grant a `once` — lending something for one load is not giving it
away — but handing it over is the same decision as reassigning it, made by the
same people. The server enforces that; hiding the option from everyone else is a
courtesy.

The picker defaults to `once` and the screen puts an explicit warning in front
of the second choice before it is pressed, naming what it hands over and saying
it is permanent. "Approve" on its own does not read like "give this away", and
the two sit one dropdown apart.

One hole closed while wiring it. An ownership grant stays 'approved' for good —
there is no single use to spend — so leaving it in approvedPartyIds() and
findApproval() would have meant an admin who later removed that person from the
record had taken nothing away: the stale approval would have gone on lending
what the removal was meant to end, and would even have been spendable on one
last order. Both now skip grantKind 'ownership'. Access to a record you were
given comes from owning it, and has to end when that does.

Worth being precise about the limit, because it is not obvious: this carries
orders only where the party is the *client*. Owning a shipper or consignee hands
over the record and nothing else, because canSeeOrder() reads clientOwner* and
nothing else. That is pre-existing and unchanged here.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory start the conversation it exists to enable
changes.body:
Looking someone up ended at their email address and their extension. The
company runs its own chat — the argument for building it here rather than
signing up for Slack — and the one screen whose whole purpose is finding a
colleague had no way to reach them through it.

Both views get it, because they are for different jobs: the cards get a "Send a
message" line beside the email, and the list puts it on the name, appearing on
hover so it does not compete with the names when running an eye down an office.
It goes on the name rather than in a column of its own on purpose — the columns
are configurable and sortable, and this is an action, with nothing to sort or
filter on.

Nothing renders for the viewer's own row, or for somebody invited who has never
signed in: there is no account on the other end, and a button that opens a
thread with yourself is not worth the row it sits on. The cards test that twice,
because Fact draws the icon and a button that rendered nothing would leave the
icon stranded on its own.

This is what needed `uid` on DirectoryPerson, which was keyed by email until
now. It is the same id chat already writes on every message, so it discloses
nothing that was not already in front of everyone.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let somebody locked out of a load ask for it, and reach whoever owns it
changes.body:
The no-access panel said "It belongs to TTL IT. Ask them to add you to it" and
gave the reader nothing to do about it. No way to say which load — they had
followed a Firestore id, which names nothing anybody says out loud — no way to
reach the owner, and no request button, because there was none to offer: the
whole approvals system was built for parties, and the panel's own comment said
so rather than rendering a button that did nothing.

So orders got the sibling collection, orderAccessRequests, alongside
partyAccessRequests. Same shape, same closed writes, same read rule, decided by
the same people in the same inbox. What differs is what approval buys, and it
differs deliberately. A party approval spends itself on one order and expires,
which keeps that audit trail one-to-one with the orders it authorized. An order
approval has nothing to be spent on — the thing being asked for is the record —
so it runs on a clock the approver picks instead: 24 hours through 30 days, or
no expiry, revocable early from Approvals.

The picker defaults to seven days and never to "no expiry". The safe direction
for a permission is the one that lapses on its own, and somebody who genuinely
wants a permanent grant should have to say so.

Expiry is applied when the grant is read, not by a job that flips the status.
There is no scheduler in this project, and a grant that outlived its clock
because a cron did not fire would be the worst failure available here. The
consequence is that a lapsed request still stores status 'approved', so
isGrantLive() is the only correct test and reading the field directly is a bug.
Said in CLAUDE.md too, because it is exactly the sort of thing the next person
gets wrong.

None of this is ownership. An approved requester can open the load; they do not
enter assignedToUids, cannot reassign it, and cannot decide anyone else's
request for it. And like the party grant, it is invisible to the rules —
orderVisible() knows nothing about it, because a rule cannot run the query. That
holds only while orders are never read from the client SDK, which is already the
rule and is now load-bearing twice over.

The panel itself now names the load, and offers a direct message and the owner's
work number beside the request. A direct thread rather than the load's own room:
that room is gated on being able to see the order, which is precisely what this
reader cannot do. The number is already on users/{uid} and readable by every
account, so it discloses nothing new.

Two smaller things found on the way in. Back went to Orders even for somebody
who arrived from Documents chasing a driver's licence — a list that, for a load
that is not theirs, does not contain it. And the Documents screen has always
linked here with ?tab=documents while this page ignored it, so following a
document landed on Details and left the reader to find the file again. Both now
follow where the reader actually came from.

Rules are deployed and verified live against ttms-59aa5: ruleset
14d34069-0939-489d-8b12-3f0d08dc0301 on cloud.firestore, matching this file,
with the orderAccessRequests block present. No new indexes — every query here
is the shape the party requests already use.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a load's paperwork stay with the people who own the load
changes.body:
storage.rules was a single `match /{allPaths=**}` allowing read and write to
anyone holding the ttlAccess claim, so every signed-in staff account could
fetch every BOL, invoice and POD in the bucket — the rate, the client and the
margin on ten thousand loads — given a path. Paths are `bols/{orderId}.pdf` and
`invoices/{orderId}.pdf`, which is to say guessable from an order id. The GET
handlers on the bol and invoice routes were the same hole with a login: they
guarded on requireCompanyUser and never asked canSeeOrder.

Rules cannot close this. They cannot read Firestore, so they cannot tell the
broker running a load from anyone else on the allowlist. The only place
ownership can be applied is the Admin SDK, which means the client SDK has to be
kept out: those three prefixes are now write-only, and reads go through GET
/api/orders/{id}/document, which applies canSeeOrder and signs a two-hour URL.
The path comes off the order document and is never taken from the request — one
visible order would otherwise mint a URL for any object in the bucket. Both
unguarded GETs are gone rather than fixed, so there is one door.

Driver's licences are deliberately exempt. A licence is checked at pickup, at
delivery, by whoever is covering the phones at 2am and by whoever chases a
detention claim a week later, none of whom is necessarily on the load, and all
of whom are on the allowlist. Narrowing it would mean a broker's day off stops
a truck.

That exemption was doing nothing, though, because the Documents screen builds
its rows from the order list, which is filtered to what the reader can see. A
licence everyone may open is no use if only its owner can find it. So licences
now come from /api/documents/licenses, the one listing that deliberately
reaches past canSeeOrder — and it redacts rather than filters. A row for a load
the reader has no access to carries the order number, the licence and who to go
and ask: no shipper, no client, no rate, no dates. Its SELECTED_FIELDS is the
guard, and widening it is how the load leaks out beside the licence.

The withheld rows name the owner in the shipper's column, with a direct message
and their US work number. A direct thread rather than the load's own room,
because that room is gated on seeing the order, which by definition this reader
is not. The phone is already on users/{uid} and readable by every signed-in
account, so nothing new is exposed; the payroll fields on the allowlist entry
must not follow it there.

Write access is unchanged and still broad: any staff account can upload to or
delete from those prefixes, because narrowing it needs the same Firestore
lookup a read cannot do. That is the lesser exposure — it costs someone the
path of a file they can no longer read back — but it is still open.

Rules are deployed and verified live against ttms-59aa5: ruleset
8df5e88f-f7a9-44ed-b6b9-2f756a8657a0 on firebase.storage, matching this file,
with no catch-all remaining. Note that rollback-rules.js --list reports the
Firestore release unless given --only storage, which makes a good storage
deploy look like it never landed.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a card that cannot be counted say so instead of reading zero
changes.body:
Four of the dashboard's counts ask Firestore for a total over a date range with
no sort. That is not an unordered query to Firestore — it sorts implicitly
ascending on the inequality field, while the index serving the same card's hover
list is descending on it. An index can be read backwards, but that reverses
every field in it, parentOrderId included, so the descending index cannot answer
the ascending form and Firestore asks for a second one differing only in
direction.

So Delivered Today, Delivered This Month, Loads Booked Today and Stale Quotes
each failed with FAILED_PRECONDITION. Every card is gathered in one Promise.all,
which took the other eight down with them, and the page had no catch: all twelve
fell back to zero and Recent Orders offered to create the first order over 10,376
of them. Active Clients read 3,717 throughout, because it is fetched separately
and touches none of those queries — one right number beside eleven wrong ones,
and nothing anywhere saying a request had failed.

The counts now carry the sort their samples already use, so one index answers
both and no new index is needed. Only correct where the range is on the sort
field: orderBy drops documents missing it, and there the inequality has dropped
them already.

The second half is that this was invisible. A failed load now says so, and the
orders panel says it could not be loaded rather than inviting you to create your
first one — an empty company and a broken page are not the same thing and should
never render the same.

Verified against the live project: the four queries return, and the cards read
10,376 active and 8,886 pending pick-up.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the party migration not undo the work that preceded it
changes.body:
Running migrate-parties.js took `parties` from one record to 7,339, which
turned two loads nobody had needed to think about into the slowest thing on the
dashboard. The Clients screen read every party — 3.7 MB, 5.8 seconds — and the
home page did the same, plus every carrier at 9 seconds, to answer three
questions: how many clients arrived this month, whose insurance is lapsing, and
what to call twenty-five client ids.

All three are now queries for what is actually wanted. The dashboard makes no
full-collection read at all; Clients, Shippers and Consignees page fifty at a
time and search a name prefix in the database, like carriers.

  Clients page       5.8s  ->  0.77s
  Dashboard summary  ~17s  ->  0.38s

The migration also stamped every party it created with the moment it ran, so
the whole book of business looked like it arrived on one day and "New Clients
This Month" read 7,339. The real dates survived as `batsCreatedAt` on the
customer rows; parties built from an order instead take their first load's date,
which is the best evidence there is of when that relationship started. All 7,339
now carry a real date spread over 2020-2026, and the card reads 1.

That correction script lifts the name-key rule out of migrate-parties.js at
runtime rather than copying it. Every party id is a hash of that function's
output, and a copy that drifted would hash to an id matching nothing and skip
the records it exists to fix — silently. Writing it out by hand once already
lost the word boundaries in the suffix rules, which is exactly that failure.

Two indexes added. Three array-field entries in firestore.indexes.json are also
repaired: they had been written with a null sort order instead of CONTAINS,
which Firestore accepted from the console but the file could not have recreated.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the client, shipper and consignee lists keep their place too
changes.body:
The last three lists still held their search box and their "only mine" toggle
in component state, so opening a party and pressing Back landed on an empty
box. Same fix as the orders and carriers lists: both go in the URL, written
with `replace` so typing leaves no history to walk back through.

One difference worth noting. Those two lists page against the database and had
to debounce; this one already holds every party it can see and filters in
memory, so the URL is written on each keystroke with no query behind it. If
this list ever pages the way the others do, it needs their debounce as well.

All three role pages share this component, so /dashboard/clients,
/dashboard/shippers and /dashboard/consignees each get it from one change.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a search and a tab survive opening a result
changes.body:
The search text and the status tab lived in component state, so a broker who
searched a customer, opened the third load and found it was the wrong one came
Back to an empty box and page one — and had to type it again to reach the
fourth. The whole point of a result list is opening more than one of them.

Both now live in the URL: /dashboard/orders?q=morris&status=booked. Back from
an order returns to the list as it was, the view is linkable into chat, and a
refresh keeps it.

Written with `replace`, not `push`, so typing does not leave a history entry
per letter — Back walks out of the list, not through it. Opening an order is
itself a push, which is what gives Back somewhere to return to.

The text box stays local state so it does not lag a keystroke behind the URL,
with the URL as the source of truth for what has actually been run; the sync
back only fires when the two genuinely differ, so it cannot fight the user
mid-word.

Carriers gets the same treatment for its search and its inactive toggle, since
its list was rebuilt the same way and would otherwise be the one place where
Back loses your place.

A default is written as an absent parameter rather than an explicit one, so a
bare /dashboard/orders still means what it always meant.

Not covered: how far down Load more has been pressed. A search narrows to a
page, which is the case this is for; restoring depth would mean replaying every
cursor in turn.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a load be found by the last four of its number
changes.body:
Numbers were indexed by prefix, like everything else, so TTL22001218 answered
to "ttl22" but not to "1218". That is backwards for how a number is actually
said: a carrier rings about "the load ending 1218" and a broker reads the last
four off a rate confirmation. Nobody recites an order number from the front.

Numbers are now indexed by every segment, so "1218", "2001" and "ttl22" all
find it. Words are left on prefixes — "morr" finds Morris, "orris" does not.
A name is something people do start at the beginning of, and segmenting every
commodity description would multiply the array for a case nobody types.

Affordable because numbers are short: about 62 stored fragments per order
becomes about 124, worst case 309 against a cap of 400, and 3.5 MB of stored
fragments becomes 6.8 across the whole collection.

Caught before the backfill was applied, so there is nothing to redo. All three
copies of the rule were run over the live collection and agree on all 10,376
orders, including on the segments.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let an order be found by any part of what it is called
changes.body:
Orders had no search box. Adding one to a page that fetched the whole
collection would have been easy and would have searched the browser's copy;
adding one to a page that fetches fifty rows would have searched those fifty
and reported nothing for a load sitting on page twelve. So the search is the
database's, like the filters beside it.

Firestore has no substring match, so each order carries `searchTerms`: every
