prefix of every word in its number, party names, lane and commodity. The query
is one array-contains, which stays flat as the collection grows — about 62
fragments per order, 245 on the worst one.

Consequences, all deliberate:

  - Prefixes only. "morr" finds Morris; "orris" does not. Storing every
    substring squares the array for a case nobody types.
  - Only the first typed word reaches Firestore. array-contains-any is an OR,
    so "palm beach" through it returns everything matching either — wider than
    what was asked. The rest of the words filter the page that comes back,
    which can leave a page shorter than its limit while more results exist.
  - searchTerms is kept out of the list projection and fetched only when a
    second word needs checking, then stripped before the rows are sent.

Searching inside a status tab stays inside it, and says so when nothing
matches — a tab is a filter people forget is on, and an empty tab and an empty
search look identical otherwise.

Every writer refreshes the fragments: createOrder inline, updateOrder through a
new route because a patch is only part of an order, and both BATS importers
after assignOrderNumbers, since the number is part of what an order is found
by. That last one is the trap carriers just fell into with nameKey — an
imported record that lists and opens perfectly well but answers to nothing in
the search box.

The rule now exists in three places, which a node script's inability to import
TypeScript makes unavoidable. All three were run over the live collection and
agree on all 10,376 orders.

Two indexes and a backfill of every order are required and are NOT applied by
committing this. See CLAUDE.md.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the lists ask for a page instead of the whole book
changes.body:
Every list screen read its entire collection on every visit. Orders was ten
thousand documents, twelve megabytes and about seventeen seconds before a row
appeared, then ninety thousand table cells for the browser to lay out; the
dashboard did the same again to work out a dozen counts by running filter over
the array. Seven screens paid that toll, and it grew with every load booked.

Now they ask for what they show:

  - /api/orders takes limit, cursor, status, the party and carrier ids,
    parentOrderId, pickupFrom and a fields projection. Orders and Carriers page
    fifty at a time behind a Load more.
  - The status tabs count with count() aggregations — about eleven document
    reads for the row rather than ten thousand.
  - The dashboard's cards are counted server-side in lib/orderSummary.ts, each
    with a capped sample for its hover list. A tooltip naming nine thousand
    loads was never read; it was just what the page happened to hold.
  - Detail screens ask about their own record instead of scanning everything to
    find three suborders or one carrier's loads.
  - Documents queries the four attachment fields. It was reading ten thousand
    orders to render a handful of rows.

Measured against production: Orders 16.9s to 0.9s, Carriers ~10s to 0.23s, the
dashboard ~17s to ~0.35s. The point is less the multiple than the shape — the
wait no longer tracks the size of the collection.

Active Clients is fetched apart from the rest. It is the one figure that cannot
be counted, since Firestore has no distinct-count, so it reads every open order
and took eight times as long as the other eleven cards together.

Carrier search moves into the database, which needs a lowercase nameKey to
match against — range queries are case-sensitive and four fifths of the
imported names are in block capitals. Both BATS importers write it too:
without that, an imported carrier would list but never answer to its name, and
a renamed one would keep answering to the name it used to have.

Search is a prefix match now. Firestore has no substring index, and the old
`includes` only worked because the collection was already in memory.

Sixteen composite indexes are required and are NOT created by committing this.
They live in firestore.indexes.json with the chat index that predates them, so
the CLI does not offer to delete it. The service account can read indexes but
not create them, so deploy them as a human — see CLAUDE.md.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a failed announcement stay quiet
changes.body:
announceOrderEvent is called with `void`, so the token lookup throwing
for a signed-out browser surfaced as an unhandled rejection on top of a
save that had already worked. The whole body is swallowed now, not just
the fetch.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let TTMS say what happened, in the room about the load
changes.body:
The alerts that already exist on the dashboard, delivered where people
are looking: carrier signed, rate confirmation sent, BOL added, status
moved, carrier assigned. The one that earns the feature on its own is
the signature — a carrier opens the link from their phone at eleven at
night, and until now nobody knew until somebody reloaded the order.

Written server-side, always. A system message carries a sender that is
not a person, and the rules pin senderUid to the caller precisely so
nobody can put words in somebody else's mouth. So every alert is posted
with the Admin SDK, from the route where the event actually happens —
the two agreements, the two documents and the signing route each post
their own.

Three events happen in the browser rather than in a route: status,
carrier, POD. Those go through /api/orders/[orderId]/announce, which
takes an event name and never message text — it re-reads the order and
describes what it finds. A route that posted text from the caller would
let anyone make TTMS say anything, in a room people trust exactly
because a person did not write it.

Nothing is posted into a room nobody has opened. A record room is made
by pressing Discuss; alerts follow the discussion rather than creating a
conversation document for every order that ever changed status. A room
opens with where the load stands, so the alerts after it read as changes
to something rather than facts out of nowhere.

Drawn as a centred line rather than a bubble, and inert — no menu, no
reactions, no thread. An automated notice shaped like a colleague is one
people answer, argue with, and then stop reading.

Discuss now opens the floating panel instead of the chat page: the whole
point of discussing a load from the load is not having to leave it.
Selecting a room the listener has not delivered yet no longer bounces
back to the conversation list, which that change would otherwise have
made visible on every click.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a room be turned down, pinned, and tied to the load it is about
changes.body:
Six things, all of them the same argument: a chat only stays useful if
the person reading it can decide what reaches them, and if the loads
being talked about are one click away rather than one search away.

Per-room notification settings, with three levels rather than a switch.
A busy room that can only be all-or-nothing gets muted on its first loud
day, and then the one message that was actually for you is lost with it.
The middle level keeps an @, a reply in a thread you are in, and a
reaction on your own words coming through, and stops everything else.

Pinned rooms and pinned threads, per person. Both, and the notification
level, live on the reader's own chatReads document — they are facts about
who is reading, not about the room, and putting them there means none of
the three needed a rules change.

Pinned messages, which are the room's rather than the reader's, as a map
keyed by message id. An array would have to be written whole, so the rule
allowing it would be allowing any member to replace every pin in the
room. This is the one part of the change that needs the rules deployed.

A Discuss button on an order, opening the room about that load. Nobody
is invited to it: whoever can see the order is entitled to be in it, and
pressing the button is what joins them — a check only the server can
make, so it happens in /api/chat/conversations before the caller's uid
goes anywhere near the membership the rules read.

Order numbers become cards, for the people allowed to see the load and
as plain text for anyone who is not. TTL numbers are matched wherever
they appear; a BATS id needs a # in front of it, because bare digits in
a freight chat are far more often a weight, a rate or a ZIP.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a thread under a file be titled by the file
changes.body:
A message may be nothing but an attachment — the type says so — but the title
stored for a thread only ever read root.text. So a thread started under a
photo or a spreadsheet was stored with an empty title, and the list rendered
an empty title as "Message deleted": the one thing it definitely was not.

Both writes now go through rootLabel, so the notification and the list agree,
and a file name stands in where there are no words. A root that really was
deleted says so explicitly rather than arriving as an empty string nobody can
tell apart from a file with no caption.

Rows written before this keep their empty title until the next reply rewrites
them, which is the ordinary cost of a copied field.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the missing-index message point at a link that is actually there
changes.body:
The thread panel told an admin to create the index "from the link in the
browser console". There was no link. Passing an error callback to onSnapshot
is precisely what stops Firestore logging the error itself, so the one place
carrying the create-index URL was being swallowed by the handler that wrote
the friendly message.

So the message sent whoever read it to a console with nothing in it, on the
one error it exists to make actionable.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let every thread you are in live in one list
changes.body:
The room list answers where everyone is talking. After threads landed there
was nothing answering what you had been asked: a reply lives under a message,
so finding the conversation you were pulled into meant remembering the room
and scrolling until a reply count changed.

"Threads I am in" spans every room, and the only record of who is in a thread
sits on the messages themselves — so it cannot be asked as a query the rules
can gate. It is written down as it happens instead: whoever writes a reply
writes a row into the list of each person that reply is for. Same trick as
lastMessage, mentionedAt and clientOwnerUids.

A document per thread rather than a map per person, which matters twice: a map
would grow towards the 1 MiB limit and need pruning, and it would mean a
colleague replying to you had to be allowed to write your whole list. This way
the rules let them write exactly one row, so the worst a member can do is put
one wrong line in somebody's list rather than empty it.

Rows are bounded rather than trusted — a row must credit the writer as the
author of the reply it describes, carry a server timestamp, and name a room
the writer is in. Deliberately not checked: whether the row's owner is still
in that room. Someone removed from a room stays in the root message's
replyUids, so that check would fail the whole reply batch rather than the one
row. Their list drops the thread at render instead, when the room name no
longer resolves — the same reason the room name is not copied onto the row.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let an answer sit under the message instead of in the room
changes.body:
Threads. A reply lands under the message it answers, and reaches the people
it is for rather than everyone: whoever wrote the message, whoever has already
replied, and anyone named with an @ in the reply. It does not move the room up
anybody's list, does not rewrite the preview line and does not mark the room
unread. Everyone else sees a reply count under the message and nothing more.

Replies live in a collection beside the messages, not as a rootId field on the
messages themselves. A Firestore equality query skips documents missing the
field, so filtering the room by rootId == null would have hidden every message
written before today, on the live database, with nowhere to test it first.

Threads keep their own read marks, so glancing at a room no longer wipes an
answer written under a message you had scrolled past.

The bubble and the composer come out of MessageThread into components of their
own, which is most of the diff. A reply has to do everything a message does —
name a colleague, carry a photo, take a pasted screenshot — and the alternative
was a second, quietly worse copy of both.

Two things this needs that code cannot do:

  - firestore.rules is edited and is NOT live until scripts/deploy-rules.js
    is run.
  - Threads need a composite index, rootId ASC + createdAt DESC on the replies
    collection. Opening a thread says so until it exists, and the browser
    console links straight to a one-click creator.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a badge say how many, and a reaction reach whoever it is for
changes.body:
Three things chat was doing badly, all of them about somebody not being
told something.

The unread dot is a number now. Counting used to mean reading every
message to add them up, which is why it was a dot; a count aggregation
is billed as one read no matter how many it counts, so "12" costs what
the dot did. The nav item, the popup bubble and the tab title are built
from the same string in ChatContext, because two badges counting
different things is how somebody opens chat to find four messages
behind a badge that said two.

A reaction now notifies the person whose message it is. Reactions live
on the message document and nobody listens to the messages of a
conversation they are not looking at, so the only person who could ever
be told was the one already staring at it. A ping on the conversation —
which every browser watches all day — carries who, what and which
message. It never marks the conversation unread: a thumbs-up is an
acknowledgement, not a thing waiting on you.

Both popovers opened where they could not be read. The alerts menu was
wider than the column it hangs in and the overflow was cut off under the
sidebar; the reaction palette was positioned inside a message list that
scrolls and clips. The palette now hangs off the viewport like
MessageActions next door, which had already solved this.

firestore.rules gains a branch for the reaction ping. Deployed.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a photo, a thumbs-up and a link do the work of a message
changes.body:
The roadmap's second stage: the small things people reach for all day, which
together are most of what separates a chat from a message board.

Reactions are a fixed set of six rather than a picker. The point of a reaction
is that it beats typing "ok", and hunting through three thousand faces does not
beat typing "ok". Hovering a count names who reacted, which is the question
actually worth asking of a dispatch note.

Photos and files by drag, paste or paperclip, uploaded as they are chosen so a
large BOL is in the bucket before the caption is finished. Images render inline
because the reason somebody sends one is for a colleague to look at it, not to
find it in a downloads folder.

Be clear about what guards an attachment: storage rules cannot read Firestore,
so the bucket is gated on the ttlAccess claim and nothing finer. Any signed-in
user who knows a file's exact path can fetch it, private room or not. The path
is written only on the message document, which IS membership-gated, and every
path carries a random id so it cannot be guessed or walked. That is the posture
the BOLs and licences have had all along, so this adds no new class of exposure
— but it is weaker than the Firestore side, and the fix if it is ever wanted is
an API route that checks membership and returns a signed URL.

Formatting uses WhatsApp's marks, not Markdown's, to match the bubbles and
because staff already have them in their fingers. Marks, links and mentions are
found in one pass — three passes is how a URL with an underscore in it comes out
half italic.

Older messages load on reaching the top, putting the reader back on the line
they were reading. The page size resets during render rather than in an effect,
or switching from a long thread to a short one would subscribe once at the old
size first and bill several hundred reads for messages thrown away a frame later.

Copy link to a message, opening the conversation with it ringed. The clipboard
fallbacks move out of CopyLinkButton into lib/clipboard.ts — the office is on
plain http, where navigator.clipboard does not exist, and a second copy button
would quietly have lacked them.

firestore.rules deployed as ruleset 655b6aaa and verified against this file:
reactions need any member to update somebody else's message, and a photo with no
caption needs the non-empty-text rule relaxed.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let chat be something you can work in rather than watch
changes.body:
Everything from the roadmap's first stage, plus the two things asking for it
straight afterwards.

Being told a message arrived: a desktop notification, a count in front of the
browser tab title, and an optional chime, all behind a bell in the conversation
list. Permission is asked on a click and never on page load — browsers punish
sites that ask unprompted. Nothing fires for the conversation already on screen,
and the first snapshot is seeded silently so a page load does not announce every
conversation that ever had a message in it.

@mentions, with the mark kept on the conversation rather than read off the last
message: a question has to still be marked when four more lines have been said
over it. Naming somebody outranks ordinary unread and shows as an @ rather than
a dot. Clicking a name opens a card with their details and a button to message
them directly — showing exactly what the Directory shows everyone and no more.

Replies quote what they answer, on anyone's message including your own. A
private reply carries the quote into a direct thread with whoever wrote it, and
can only ever be addressed to that person, which is what makes carrying the
room's name across safe. The quote stores a copy but renders the live original
wherever there is one, so deleting a message blanks its quotes in the room it
was said in.

Messages are bubbles now, yours on the right and everyone else's on the left,
with the actions on a menu hanging off the bubble instead of a row of unlabelled
icons at the far edge of the thread.

Editing is allowed where it was not before. The original objection was that a
message somebody has acted on should not silently become something else;
`editedAt` is pinned to the server clock and the thread says "(edited)", which
removes the silently rather than the edit.

firestore.rules deployed as ruleset de789350 and verified against this file.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let everyone talk to each other without leaving TTMS
changes.body:
Chat between staff: the company room everyone is in, direct threads, and
named rooms with a chosen membership. On its own page and in a panel that
floats over every other one, because the questions people ask each other
are nearly always about the record already on screen.

Both views share one set of listeners through ChatProvider, so what is open
and what has been read cannot drift apart between them — and the unread
badge in the nav counts the same conversations rather than opening a second
set to count them again.

This is the first part of the app that reads Firestore live from the
browser. That is safe here and is not safe for orders: "conversations I am
a member of" is a single array-contains query the rules can check exactly,
whereas the order union cannot be expressed as one query at all. Creating a
conversation and changing who is in it still go through /api/chat.

firestore.rules is edited and NOT deployed — run scripts/deploy-rules.js or
chat stays dark for everyone.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a link to somebody else's record say whose it is
changes.body:
A link to an order or a client is the obvious way to hand one to a colleague,
and it already worked for anyone who could see the record. For anyone who
could not, both pages rendered "not found" — false in the case that actually
happens. The record exists and belongs to somebody, and two people would then
spend ten minutes deciding whether a load had been deleted.

getOrder and getParty answered null for both "gone" and "not yours", so the
pages had nothing to tell them apart with. They return one of three answers
now, and readOrder/readParty on the server hand back the owner's name with the
refusal. getVisibleOrder and getVisibleParty stay on as the throwing face of
those, so the routes that only ever serve the record did not have to move.

The client page was reading its document straight from Firestore, which is why
a denial arrived as a bare permission error with nothing in it. It goes through
a new /api/parties/{partyId} now, the way the client list already did.

Asking for access needed the id, which /api/parties/resolve deliberately
refuses to hand out. Accepting one here widens nothing: the request is still
the owner's to approve, and an id on its own has never been the thing that
grants access. What differs is where the caller got it — resolve answers
somebody fishing with a typed name, this answers somebody sent a URL by a
person who could already see the record. Both write to partyAccessProbes,
now tagged with which of the two it was.

Approving one grants a little more than "let me look": the existing approval
lends visibility until it is spent on an order. Rather than leave that to be
discovered afterwards, the panel says so before you send, and the inbox
separates wanting to open a record from wanting to use one.

Orders get the panel and no button. There is no equivalent of
partyAccessRequests for them yet, and a button that filed nothing would be
worse than the sentence naming who to ask. Carriers needed neither half of
this: every signed-in user can already read every carrier.

Copy link sits next to Edit on all three, and falls back twice — execCommand,
then the URL in a box to copy by hand. navigator.clipboard does not exist
outside a secure context, and staff reach this over plain http on the office
network, so the button would have silently done nothing on most desks.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let Settings stand two columns wide instead of one long scroll
changes.body:
Overview, Organization and Operations each stacked their panels down one
narrow column, so reaching the last one meant scrolling past all of the
others. They now sit in two columns, splitting by height rather than by
meaning: the tall panel on each tab takes a column of its own.

Nothing got narrower. The page frame widens for these tabs the way the
People tab already did, and two columns at that width come out at about
the width the single column had. Below xl there is not room for two
readable columns and it falls back to the stack it was.

The panels each carried their own top or bottom margin, which read as a
ragged gap once they sat side by side; the pages now own that spacing,
which also retires the -mt-6 the Organization page needed to cancel it.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory list be narrowed to the columns you need
changes.body:
The full table is wider than a laptop screen once the admin columns are on
it, and most of the time somebody scanning it wants two of them. A Columns
button over the list switches the rest off; the button says how many are
off, so a column that is missing is explainable rather than mysterious.

Which columns exist now lives in lib/directoryColumns.ts rather than in the
table, beside the sorting and for the same reason: the page owns what is on
screen. The URL carries the hidden columns rather than the shown ones, so a
plain /dashboard/directory is still the whole table, and a column added
later appears for everyone instead of staying invisible to whoever has an
old link saved.

The table now draws the list it is handed, one cell per column key in a
typed map, so a column without a cell is a compile error. What it replaced
was a header row and a body row that each decided separately what to draw —
which held only while nothing could be switched off.

If the column being sorted on is hidden, by the picker or by a pasted link,
the order falls back to name: rows in an order with no heading and no arrow
to explain it look shuffled. It is worked out on the way past rather than
written to the URL, so switching the column back on restores the order.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the People tab fold down to the part you came for
changes.body:
The three sections here — a form, the directory and the removal archive — were
one long scroll, and only one of them is what any given visit is about. All
three now fold shut, remembering the choice per browser: Add People and Removed
People start closed, the directory starts open.

Sub-tabs were the other way to do it and were rejected. The Overview cards, the
settings search box and its "jump to this person" results all deep-link by URL
hash, and every one of those links would have had to learn which sub-tab to
switch to first. Instead scrollToAnchor announces a jump before it scrolls and
the section holding the target opens itself — an event rather than a call,
because a jump within the tab you are already on is a pushState, which fires no
hashchange for anything to hear. A section settles its state once on arrival,
or the hash left sitting in the address bar would keep re-opening a section
that had just been folded away.

The folding is CollapsibleSection, lifted out of the removal log, which had the
only one of these. Children are not rendered while a section is shut, so the
log keeps loading its rows on first open rather than on every visit.

While in here, the two sections that were a single narrow column now use the
width they are given:

- Add People runs in two columns — addresses and the settings that hold true
  for all of them on the left, the one-person details on the right, three
  fields abreast on a wide screen.
- Removed People lists two entries side by side. A removal is a name and a
  date, so a single column left most of the row empty.
- Both were capped narrower than the directory between them, which read as a
  mistake rather than a decision. All three run to the same edge now.

Everything stacks back into one column below the breakpoint.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the access list be narrowed to one office or team
changes.body:
The Status and Permissions rows made it quick to ask "who is suspended" or
"who is finance", but not "who works in Miami" — the only way to answer that
was to read every row. Sites and teams are already on each person, so the
same tiles answer it.

Both rows only appear once there is something to filter by, and the
unassigned tile only when somebody is actually missing one — otherwise it is
a tile that can only ever empty the list.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory list be sorted by any column
changes.body:
Every heading in the list view is a button now: click it to order by that
column, click it again to reverse. An arrow marks the column in use and
which way round it is; a faint one appears under the pointer elsewhere so
it is clear the headings can be clicked at all.

The rules live in lib/directorySort.ts rather than in the table, next to
the searching and filtering the page already does. Blanks sink to the
bottom of both directions — half the company has no start date, and an
ascending sort that opened with a screen of dashes would hide what it was
asked to show. Extensions compare as numbers so 9 precedes 10, dates
compare as dates, and ties fall back to name so reversing the offices
does not also shuffle the people inside each one.

The order rides in the URL beside the view and the two filters, so it
survives a refresh and "the Dallas list, oldest hires first" is something
one person can paste to another. Cards keep name order: they have no
columns, and re-ordering them by an extension nobody can see on a card
would read as the page shuffling itself.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Make signing a link a single, all-or-nothing step
changes.body:
The route read the token to check whether it had been used, then wrote the
result as a separate round trip. Nothing held the document still in between,
so two submissions of the same link could both see "unsigned" and both write.
The second silently overwrote the first: two people signed, one name survived
in the audit trail, and neither was told. The form's disabled button does not
cover this, being per-browser, and the link can be forwarded or posted directly.

Burning the link and advancing the order were also two independent writes. If
the first succeeded and the second failed, the carrier was told they had
signed, the order still said they had not, and the link refused to work again.

Both now happen inside one transaction, along with the validity checks, so
they either all take effect or none do. A SignError carries the status out of
the callback, since it can only signal failure by throwing; the carrier sees
the same messages and codes as before.

The timestamp is taken outside the transaction on purpose — Firestore may run
the callback again when the token is contended, and the signature should
record when the carrier submitted, not which retry won.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let the directory be scanned as a list, and filtered by clicking
changes.body:
Cards are good for finding a colleague you cannot spell; they are poor
for running an eye down a whole office looking for an extension. There
is now a Cards/List switch, and the list puts every field in the same
column on every row.

Clicking an office or a team in the list filters down to it, and
clicking it again clears it. Only those two columns do this — they are
the only ones where a value repeats, so filtering on an extension or an
address would leave the one row you were already looking at. A team
dropdown joins the office one, because a filter you can switch on has to
be one you can see and switch off.

The view and both filters travel in the URL, so a refresh keeps your
place and the Dallas list is a link you can paste to someone.

Admins and HR also see the four fields that were being loaded and thrown
away: legal name, personal email, start date and date of birth. This
needed nothing loosened. Those fields live only on allowedUsers, which
admin and HR alone can read, and are deliberately never mirrored onto
users/{uid} — so for everyone else they are absent rather than hidden,
and MIRRORED_FIELDS is untouched. The note at the top of lib/directory.ts
now spells out why that distinction is the thing to keep hold of.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Make the photo big enough to recognise someone, and clickable to see properly
changes.body:
A directory is read by looking for a face, and a 40px circle is small for that.
Photos are 64px on a directory card and 48px in the access list, and the
initial shown when someone has no photo is now sized off the circle rather than
fixed — a big circle with `text-sm` in it looked empty.

Clicking a photo opens it full size over the page with the person's name under
it. Escape, the backdrop and the close button all dismiss it: a picture
covering the screen with no visible way out is alarming.

Only a real photo is clickable. An initial is the same initial at any size, so
that circle stays plain.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Show everyone which office and team a colleague is in
changes.body:
The Directory held the office and the team back for admin and HR, which left a
broker with a phone number and no idea which building the person is in. Both
are ordinary working information — a site and a team grant nothing, which is
why any signed-in user may already read those two collections — so they are
now on every card, and the office filter is there for everyone too.

The second phone number stays admin and HR only. It is usually someone's
personal mobile in their home country rather than a desk they sit at, which is
a different kind of fact from the rest of the card.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Give everyone a company phone book, and show each role only what it needs
changes.body:
Settings is the access list — who may sign in, what they may do, and the
payroll details behind them — and stays admin and HR only. There was nowhere
for an ordinary broker to look up a colleague's extension.

Directory is that page: open to everyone who can sign in, read-only, with the
email address and the phone numbers clickable, because dialling is half the
reason to open a phone book at all.

A broker sees the name, company email, US work line and extension. Admin and
HR see the same cards with the second number, the office and the team filled
in, plus anyone who has been set up but has never signed in — a new hire's
desk number is in the system on their first day. Suspended people are absent
for everyone else and marked for those two.

Two sources on purpose: `users/{uid}` for everyone, which every signed-in user
may already read and which carries exactly the ordinary directory fields, and
the allowlist for admin and HR, which they may already read and which also
holds the people with no uid yet.

The narrowing is decided in lib/directory.ts rather than in the page, and the
note there says plainly what it is not: those fields are readable by any
signed-in account under the existing rules and always have been. The real
boundary is MIRRORED_FIELDS — legal name, date of birth, personal email and
start date never reach the profile everyone can read. No rules changed.

The Handbook's "admin-only fields" callout said start date was visible to
everyone. It is not, and never was; corrected alongside.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Lay people out as cards, and stop cutting the office name off
changes.body:
The access list was one full-width row per person down a narrow column, so
two dozen people were a long scroll with half of every row left empty. The
People tab now takes the whole screen and lays people out two abreast; the
other four tabs stay narrow, because a form field stretched across a wide
monitor is harder to fill in, not easier.

Each person's details used to be joined into one line ending in `truncate`,
which quietly cut whatever sat last — the office name, every time. They are
now one fact per line, none of them truncated, behind a shared Fact component
so that decision lives in one place.

Status moves into a chip in the card's corner rather than a line of its own,
and editing someone takes the full width with the form in three columns, so
the editor got shorter too.

HR now sees each person's roles as plain chips. The whole role row used to be
hidden from them along with the buttons, so HR could not see who was an admin.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Accept a Mexican number that still carries the old mobile prefix
changes.body:
Mexico dropped the +52 1 / 044 / 045 mobile prefixes in 2019, but they are
still saved in the contact cards and call logs numbers get copied from, so
+52 1 442 755 9621 was arriving as eleven digits and being refused.

Those prefixes are now stripped, alone or behind the country code, but only
when exactly ten digits are left over — a real number that happens to start
with a 1 is already the right length and is untouched.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Type dates the way the setting says, not the way the browser does
changes.body:
The date format setting stopped at the edge of every entry box, because
<input type="date"> takes its format from the browser's language and will
not be told otherwise. A person editing a user saw 03/04/2020 in the box
and 4-Mar-2020 everywhere around it.

DateField replaces all fourteen of them: orders, carriers, the people
editor, Add People and the import row editor. The text is ours and shows
the company format; the calendar button opens the browser's real picker,
which is the half worth keeping. Value in and out is still YYYY-MM-DD, so
no form or API knows the difference.

parseDateInput() reads what was typed, using the setting to settle whether
3/4/2020 is March or April. Under the spelled-month format nobody has said
which, so that one is refused as ambiguous rather than guessed — the same
rule the spreadsheet importer already follows. Nothing is stored until the
text is a real date, so a mistyped one cannot be saved as if it were meant.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let an admin choose how dates are written, and write them one way everywhere
changes.body:
Adds appSettings/general.dateFormat, chosen in Settings -> Operations ->
Date Format: day with the month spelled out (4-Mar-2020, the default),
MM/DD/YYYY, or DD/MM/YYYY. Company-wide rather than per person, because
brokers read each other's orders.

Eight pages each carried their own copy of the same date formatter, which
was harmless until the format became a choice — one setting cannot reach
eight copies, and a screen left behind showing 03/04 next to one showing
04/03 is the confusion the setting exists to end. They now all go through
src/lib/dateFormat.ts, via useDateFormatters() in components.

Documents are deliberately excluded: the BOL, the invoice, the carrier
agreement and the public signing page keep spelling the month out. They
leave the company, and a slashed date is two different days depending on
who is holding the paper.

Also teaches the spreadsheet importer to read 25-Nov-2000, which is how
the HR sheets are kept. Numeric day-first dates are still refused — with
no month name there is no safe way to tell 11/12 apart.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let someone's second phone number be Mexican as well as Guatemalan
changes.body:
The second number was Guatemala or nothing, stored in a field called
phoneGt. It is now one field with the country beside it — phoneOther +
phoneOtherRegion — shown on the forms as one "Other phone" box with a
country picker. A field per country would have grown with every hire
from somewhere new and left everyone else a row of empty boxes.

Mexican numbers are ten digits, the same as US ones, so the region is
now structurally impossible to infer from the digits. It was already
never guessed; that reasoning is written down in lib/phone.ts.

The spreadsheet keeps a column per country, and gains "Mexico phone".
A file has no dropdown, so the heading is what says which country the
digits are. A row filling both country columns is refused rather than
guessed at, and says why.

Nothing in Firestore had to change for this to be correct: everything
reads the number through otherPhone(), which understands both shapes,
and every write clears the old field. scripts/migrate-phone-other.js
moves the records nobody has re-saved — dry run reports four, all
Guatemala. It has not been run.

No security rules were touched, so nothing needs deploying.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Split Settings into five tabs, each with its own address
changes.body:
Settings was one page with nine panels stacked down it, so reaching anything
meant scrolling past everything. The panels themselves are unchanged; they are
now spread across Overview, People, Organization, Operations and Data.

Each tab is a real route rather than a piece of state, so it can be linked to,
bookmarked and gone back from. The tab bar lives in a layout, which does not
re-render between the pages under it, and reads the active tab from the URL
only — a state copy would start lying the first time someone used Back.

Overview is the landing tab: every panel as a card showing what it is currently
set to, since the usual question about most of these is what it says rather
than let me change it. It deliberately does not count Removed People — that
archive holds dates of birth and personal emails, and printing a number would
fetch them on every visit.

A search box in the layout covers the cost of tabs, which is having to know
which tab a thing is on. It matches panels by what they do as well as by name,
and people by name or email, jumping to their row. The directory behind the
people half is fetched lazily on the first keystroke.

The access check moved into the layout, so a tab added later cannot skip it. HR
still sees People and nothing else, with no tab bar drawn and the Overview
redirecting them there.

The handbook and the in-app handbook page now name the tab in every
"Settings -> X" instruction, and no longer tell anyone to scroll.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let work groups be renamed, and show which page you are on
changes.body:
Two small things people kept tripping over in Settings and the sidebar.

Renaming a work group. A group could be created and deleted but never
renamed, so a typo in a name meant deleting the group and rebuilding it
from scratch — which detaches every client, shipper, consignee and order
that group owned. The save endpoint already accepted a new name; there
was simply no button for it. There is now a pencil on each row, matching
the one on Teams directly above it: the name becomes a text box, the
green tick saves, the grey X cancels, Enter saves and Escape cancels.

A rename changes the label only. Records point at the group's id, not
its name, so nothing moves and nobody's access changes.

Renaming and editing members are deliberately separate modes, and
opening one closes the other. They would otherwise compete for the same
row, and somebody fixing a typo has no reason to be shown a member list.

Highlighting the current page. Every sidebar item looked identical, so
the nav gave no clue where you were. The current one now keeps the
lighter blue background and white text instead of showing it only on
hover, and carries aria-current="page" for screen readers.

Sub-pages count as their section, so opening a single order keeps Orders
lit rather than dropping the highlight entirely. Dashboard is matched
exactly instead of by prefix — every page in the app lives under
/dashboard, so a prefix test would leave Dashboard lit on every screen.

npm run build passes.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Give orders real sequence numbers, and keep the BATS number in front
changes.body:
Order numbers used to be four random digits: TTL-2026-4821. There were only
9,000 of them and nothing checked whether one was already in use, so two
different loads would have ended up sharing a number somewhere around the few
hundredth order of the year. The number also said nothing about when a load was
booked.

Orders now get TTL + the year counted from 2000 + a six-digit running count:
TTL26000042. The count restarts each January. Because the year comes first and
the count is a fixed width, sorting the numbers as plain text puts them in the
order the loads were created - no extra field, no parsing. In 2100 the year part
becomes 100 rather than wrapping to 00, so the first load of that year is
TTL100000001.

How a number is handed out

The next number lives in one small document per year, counters/orderNumber-2026,
and is handed out by a Firestore transaction behind a new guarded route,
POST /api/orders/number.

It has to be a stored counter rather than "one past the highest so far": that is
a question two brokers pressing Save in the same second can both answer the same
way, and they would get the same number. The counter is closed to the browser in
firestore.rules, because anything that could write it could wind it back and
reissue a number already printed on a carrier's rate confirmation.

A number is spent the moment it is drawn, so a save that fails afterwards leaves
a gap in the sequence. That is deliberate. Reissuing the skipped number would
let two loads carry one number across BOLs and invoices; gaps cost nothing,
since the numbers still sort.

Historical orders

Every order already in the system now has a sequence number too, assigned in the
order the loads were actually created, year by year. scripts/backfill-order-
numbers.js does that in one pass over the whole collection, with --dry-run.

It is a separate pass rather than part of the import because an import only sees
the rows in one CSV - importing 2024 after 2023 would have given the older loads
the higher numbers. Sorting is by createdAt, which for a BATS order is the BATS
order date, not the day it was imported. Same-day ties are broken by BATS id,
which is itself sequential, because many exported rows carry a date with no
time.

The BATS import numbers new rows as they arrive, by the same rule.

Both refuse to renumber an order that already has a sequence number, which is
what makes them safe to re-run. Once a number is on a rate confirmation in a
carrier's file, it cannot move.

Which number a load is shown under

Having a sequence number is not the same as leading with it. A BATS-era load
still goes by its BATS id - on its header, in every list, and on the BOL,
invoice and rate confirmation that go out under it. The company worked those
loads under that number for years: it is what a carrier has in their file, what
a client puts on a remittance, and what a broker types into a search. Loads
booked in TTMS lead with their sequence number.

orderDisplayNumber() in src/types/order.ts is that rule, and all fourteen places
that show an order number now go through it instead of reading the field
directly - an if-statement in fourteen places is how a rate confirmation
eventually goes out with the wrong number on it. orderAltNumber() gives the
load's other number, shown underneath, never instead. The documents search
matches on either, because staff search by both.

Two conventions therefore run side by side, permanently. That is a split along a
line that already exists, between the old system and this one, and it settles
itself as BATS-era loads close out.

Nothing was lost

- The BATS id is untouched in batsId, and now appears on the order page on
  purpose. It used to be visible only because it WAS the order number.
- Whatever an order was called before is kept in previousOrderNumber, which is
  the only home the old TTL-2026-4821 numbers have.

One thing worth flagging for anyone reading this later: orderNumber was briefly
added to the import's PRESERVE list, which forces the stored value
unconditionally. That would have pinned every historical order to the BATS id it
arrived with and made retroactive numbering impossible. It needs the conditional
treatment in RECONCILE instead - keep a real sequence number, give way to a BATS
id. Both copies of the import were fixed.

Verified with npm run build and a standalone test of the numbering logic
(ordering, same-day tie-breaks, the 2100 roll, and that a BATS id can never be
mistaken for a sequence number). The backfill and the rules deploy have both
been run against production.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let each user set their own column widths on the Orders table
changes.body:
The Orders list has columns whose useful width differs per person and per
day: Commodity can be a one-line vehicle description or a paragraph of
equipment, while Client and Pickup are usually narrow. A single fixed
layout suits nobody, so let the user drag the divider between two headings
and keep what they chose.

Widths are a personal display preference, not company data, so they persist
in localStorage rather than Firestore - one broker widening a column must
not change what anyone else sees, and it is not worth a write to the live
database on every drag.

The table switches to `table-fixed`. Under the default auto layout the
browser re-measures each column against its content and silently overrides
whatever was dragged. The consequence is that cells now clip or wrap
instead of stretching their column, and the card scrolls sideways when the
columns total more than the window - which is what makes a genuinely wide
Commodity column possible.

The drag handle is a focusable separator, so the columns can also be sized
with the arrow keys.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let a team be led by someone who has not signed in yet
changes.body:
A team's lead was stored as `leadUid` and the picker was built from
`users/{uid}` — so only people who had already signed in could be named.
That is backwards for how teams actually get set up: the lead is very
often the new manager the team is being built around, and the whole team
read as leaderless until their first day.

Teams now hold a lead either way. `leadUid` stays the preferred shape,
because a uid survives an address change; `leadEmail` holds the address
until a uid exists. At most one is ever set. This is the same holding
pattern work groups already use for `memberEmails`, and
claimPendingAssignments() drains it at first sign-in in the same pass
that claims their clients, orders and groups — so nothing downstream has
to match on both fields for long.

- src/types/team.ts — `leadEmail`, plus findTeamLead() so every reader
  resolves a lead the same way instead of testing one field.
- src/lib/teamLead.ts (new) — resolveLead(), shared by POST /api/teams
  and PATCH /api/teams/[teamId]. The picker now names a lead by email,
  the one identifier everybody on the allowlist has, and the server
  decides which field to write. Still checked against the allowlist
  rather than trusted from the picker, which can be stale by submit.
  It lives in lib because a route file should only export handlers.
- src/lib/pendingClaims.ts — claims teams led by email; equality query,
  since a team has exactly one lead.
- DELETE /api/admin/users — clears a team's lead by email as well as by
  uid, and now runs even when there is no uid. A lead who never signed
  in is held by email alone, and is exactly the person most likely to be
  removed before their first day; previously that team would have kept
  pointing at an address no longer on the system.
- TeamsPanel — the picker lists the allowlist, marking who is pending or
  suspended, and a team's row says "(has not signed in yet)" beside a
  lead who cannot open TTMS yet. That is a choice worth surfacing, not a
  thing to discover weeks later.

Putting a pending person *on* a team already worked — `teamId` lives on
the allowlist entry — so nothing changed there.

No firestore.rules change: `teams` is already `write: false` and every
write goes through the API. No new composite index — `leadEmail` is a
single-field equality match.

Verified with `npm run build` (the only automated check that exists).

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Keep BATS master links and first-available pickup, and add managed lead sources
changes.body:
Three BATS columns were being read past and dropped. MasterOrderId now sets
parentOrderId, so an imported suborder shows under its master instead of
looking standalone. FirstAvailablePickup gets a field of its own, kept separate
from pickupDate because it is the client's constraint and does not move, while
pickupDate is what dispatch scheduled.

parentOrderId had to move out of PRESERVE for the link to ever land. PRESERVE
lets any stored value beat the CSV, null included, and every already-imported
order holds null there — so a refresh would have kept re-applying it and no
historical suborder would have been linked. It reconciles now: a value set in
the TMS wins, an empty one gives way to BATS.

SourceName and LeadSourceName become a managed list rather than free text.
Typed by hand the same source arrives three ways and reports on it are
worthless, so leadSources is admin-maintained reference data that the import
seeds from the names it finds and matches records against, leaving an imported
order or client with its source already selected.

Records store only sourceId; the label resolves from the list at render time,
so a rename lands everywhere without rewriting thousands of documents. The raw
BATS text stays on the record as a fallback label for names that matched
nothing.

Setting a source is narrower than editing the record: admins and the record's
own owners only, since attribution is what commission gets argued over.
Anyone who can see an order can otherwise edit it, dispatch and finance
included. canEditSource() is mirrored into firestore.rules, and a retired
source keeps working on records that carry it — deleting one anything still
points at is refused.

Note the next import rewrites every order rather than only changed rows: the
new fields change the row hash that decides what to skip.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Switch the git rule to committing straight to main
changes.body:
CLAUDE.md said to branch off main and open a PR. This repo is worked solo
and reviewed in the editor, so a branch only adds a merge step that buys
nothing. Erwin asked for commits to go straight to main.

The rest of the rule is unchanged: still only commit when asked, and still
never commit .env.local or the service-account JSON.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Make orders and clients owned records, assigned during BATS import
changes.body:
Ownership arrives in the BATS export as a rep's name and, until now, stayed
a name. Nothing turned it into access. This resolves owners during the
import itself, gives orders real ownership for the first time, and keeps a
permanent record of every owner a record has held.

Fixes a live leak
-----------------
importOrdersCSVs registered the client/shipper/consignee parties with no
owner at all, even though it read AssignedTo for the order. Any client that
first appeared in the orders CSV therefore landed unowned, and an unowned
party is visible to every signed-in user. It now passes the rep through.

Resolution at import time
-------------------------
New src/lib/ownerResolution.ts turns a BATS name into user ids, work group
ids, or an email. Matching runs against `allowedUsers`, not `users`:
existing is the test, not having signed in. Somebody invited last week who
has never logged in is assigned for real, held under `assignedToEmails`
until first sign-in mints a uid to convert it to. Work groups own records;
teams remain the org chart and are deliberately not matched. "Gabe/Axel"
splits into two owners. Ambiguity is never guessed - two candidates leaves
the record as text for an admin to settle, because a wrong owner silently
hands one broker another broker's book of business.

Names matching nobody stay as text (`assignedToName` on a party,
`assignedTo` on an order) and are recorded in the history as a `text` owner
that grants nothing, until an admin or dispatcher assigns someone.

Orders are now owned, and closed by default
-------------------------------------------
firestore.rules previously read `allow read, create, update, delete: if
isAllowedUser()` - every signed-in user, every order, no filter.

Two independent routes in now: the order's own owners, and the owners of
its client. The client cascade cannot be evaluated in rules - they cannot
query, and a get() on the client party per order would exceed the
20-document-access limit on any list - so the client's owners are mirrored
onto each order as clientOwnerUids/clientOwnerGroupIds and refreshed by
syncClientOwners() whenever a client changes hands.

An order with no owner is visible only to admin/dispatch/finance. This is
deliberately stricter than a party, where unowned means shared reference
data: an unowned party is usually an unclaimed facility, an unowned order
is a live load with rates on it.

Reads moved behind /api/orders. The union of "mine, my groups', my
clients'" cannot be expressed as one client-SDK query the rules would
approve. listOrders()/getOrder() were the single choke point all seven
order-reading pages use, so they inherited the filtering unchanged.

Ownership history
-----------------
orders/{id}/ownerEvents and parties/{id}/ownerEvents keep every owner a
record has ever had, with actor, IP and timestamp. A subcollection rather
than an array so the log cannot be rewritten by a document update and
cannot grow the parent without bound. Closed to the client SDK entirely -
inside a subcollection match `resource.data` is the event, not the parent,
so the visibility helpers would test the wrong document and fall through to
their "nobody owns this" branch. Read it through the owners routes instead.

The import writes the opening entry for every record it creates, so the
timeline starts at the source rather than at the first manual edit.

Closes a self-serve ownership hole
----------------------------------
updateParty wrote assignedToUids straight from the browser, and the rules
allowed any update by anyone who could see the record. Since unowned
parties are visible to everyone, any broker could claim any unclaimed
client and lock the rest of the company out of it, leaving no trace.

Ownership now moves only through /api/{orders,parties}/{id}/owners, limited
to admins and dispatchers, writing the history entry in the same batch. The
rules enforce it too via ownershipUnchanged().

People who have not signed in
-----------------------------
Work groups hold pending members in `memberEmails`; parties and orders hold
pending owners in `assignedToEmails`. claimPendingAssignments() drains all
three at first sign-in, before the profile write, so group membership is
mirrored onto users/{uid}.groupIds in time for the first page load.

These fields had to join every "is this unowned?" test - in canSeeParty(),
in partyVisible(), and in the listVisibleParties query - or a record held
for a not-yet-signed-in rep would read as public.

Settings now lists people from the allowlist rather than from `users`, so
an admin can build out a work group or a team before a new hire's first
day. Team membership already flowed through allowedUsers.teamId; only the
member count needed widening.

Dead rules removed
------------------
firestore.rules carried `documents` subcollection rules under orders,
parties, shippers and carriers granting every signed-in user read and write.
docs/schema-guide.md describes that subcollection, but it was never built -
attachments are Storage files whose paths sit on the order. Rules removed,
schema guide marked NOT IMPLEMENTED so nobody reinstates them from the doc.

Known gap, not addressed here
-----------------------------
Restricting an order does not restrict its files. storage.rules cannot read
Firestore, so the bucket is gated only on the ttlAccess claim: any signed-in
user can read every BOL, invoice, POD and driver's licence, and
bols/{orderId}.pdf and invoices/{orderId}.pdf are fully deterministic paths.
Pre-existing, now inconsistent with the rest. Plan written up separately.

Duplicated logic
----------------
The matcher exists three times - ownerResolution.ts plus mirrors in
scripts/import-bats.js and scripts/resolve-party-owners.js - because plain
node scripts cannot import TypeScript, the same reason the importer is
already duplicated. Leaving the CLI importer alone would have had it write
ownerless records over owned ones, which is the drift its banner already
warns about. CLAUDE.md's keep-in-sync table covers all of it.

Verified: npm run build compiles; tsc --noEmit clean; both scripts pass
node --check; deploy-rules.js --dry-run validates.

NOT DEPLOYED. firestore.rules changes nothing until scripts/deploy-rules.js
runs. Rollback point before deploying: 51fb0c15-3438-464d-aee6-c2d6439b87e9

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Remember Google mileage per lane so each lane is only billed once
changes.body:
Google Routes bills per lookup, so the same warehouse pair was charged
again on every order that used it, and every pre-existing order billed a
lookup the first time somebody opened it. Lane mileage is now written
down permanently the first time Google answers, and read back from there
forever after.

New collection laneDistances/{hash}, Admin SDK only. The id is a SHA-256
of the normalized address pair. Direction is deliberately not collapsed:
A-to-B and B-to-A differ on one-way segments and divided highways, and
merging them would serve a number Google never returned.

Only confirmed Google answers are stored. The free estimate stays out of
the cache on purpose - it costs nothing to recompute, so caching it would
trade a Firestore read for arithmetic, and it would freeze the output of
a formula that is expected to be retuned, leaving two calibrations live
at once with no way to tell them apart. Per-order stability already lives
on the order's own laneMiles field.

The cache write is gated on the Routes call returning ok, never on the
response merely being returnable. Writing down a degraded fallback would
pin a lane to an estimate permanently, and fixing the billing afterwards
would not bring it back.

Nothing re-asks Google on its own. An admin can force one lane at a time
from the order's distance panel, behind a confirm that says it costs a
lookup. That route requires admin, refuses to run unless the company is
actually on Routes mode - so it cannot bill against a setting that says
estimate - and leaves the stored mileage untouched if Google fails.

Every recheck is logged forever in laneDistances/{hash}/refreshes: who,
when, the previous mileage and the new one, and which order it was
triggered from. Mileage may already sit on a quote or an invoice, so
"who changed 525 to 540, and when" has to survive the next change. Only
the order the admin is looking at is updated; other orders on the same
lane keep what they were quoted on.

Known gap, deliberately left: orders that stored an estimate before the
mode was switched keep it, and show no refresh button. Converting those
needs a separate backfill script and would bill one lookup per distinct
lane.

firestore.rules denies both the lane docs and the refresh log to clients.
NOT LIVE until scripts/deploy-rules.js is run. Belt-and-braces only -
unmatched paths already default-deny.

Verified with npm run build; no test suite exists. Not yet exercised
against the live Routes API.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Store phone numbers in one shape and fix bad import rows in place
changes.body:
Phone numbers were stored exactly as typed, so the same line could sit in
the directory three ways depending on who entered it and whether it came
in through the form or a spreadsheet. All three entry points now read
them through one normalizer: US numbers are stored as +(469) 935-4100 and
Guatemala numbers as +(502) 4874-0227, with or without the country code
and whatever the punctuation.

The test is digit count and nothing else -- 10 for US, 8 for Guatemala.
A number that is the right length is reformatted; anything else is left
blank and reported rather than stored half-read. There is no area-code
validation on purpose: a real number wrongly refused is worse than a
wrong one let through, because an admin can see and fix a wrong number
and cannot see one that silently vanished.

In the spreadsheet importer a bad phone is the one thing that does not
reject its row -- the rest of the person saves and only the number is
left out, and on someone who already has a number the good one is kept.
Everywhere else the number is saved blank, with the field warning about
it before the save and the response naming it again afterwards.

The import results screen can now fix a row without going back to Excel.
Every row opens the whole person, with the box that caused the problem
outlined and the reason under it; site, team and roles are pickers so the
same mistake cannot recur, and a column the file does not have is added
on demand. It edits the spreadsheet rather than the directory, so the
plan on screen goes stale and has to be checked again before anything can
be applied -- corrections go through the same validation as the original
upload instead of a second write path.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Record payroll names, group people into teams, and add an HR role
changes.body:
Three related additions to the people directory.

Full legal name (`legalName`) is the name as it appears on payroll, for
the people whose everyday name is not the one on the form. It is stored
on the allowlist entry and deliberately NOT mirrored onto `users/{uid}`,
which every signed-in user can read — it joins date of birth, personal
email and start date behind the admin-only boundary. It appears in the
row editor, the Add People form, the CSV export, the import template and
the removal archive.

Teams (`teams/{id}`) record who someone reports to: a name and a lead,
assignable per person alongside their site. Modelled on sites, and like
sites they are NOT an access boundary — nothing in firestore.rules reads
`teamId`. Work groups remain the thing that shares records between
people. Keeping the two apart is the point: recording that someone
reports to a manager must never hand them that manager's book of
business. Deleting a team detaches its members; removing a person clears
them as any team's lead.

The HR role (`isHr`) grants read-only access to this directory and
nothing else, because payroll staff need the legal names but have no
business in the brokers' records. HR can open Settings, read every entry
including the payroll fields, and export the list; every control that
writes is absent for them. It is deliberately excluded from
canSeeAllParties(), and has no custom claim — nothing in either rules
file reads one, so the profile lookup is enough.

The import template gains Full legal name and Team columns. A bare "Full
name" header is deliberately not accepted as an alias for the legal name,
and "Group" is not accepted for Team — the first would file everyone's
everyday name as their payroll name, the second collides with work
groups.

firestore.rules changes here are NOT live until deployed with
scripts/deploy-rules.js. The `allowedUsers` read rule is what actually
enforces HR access.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Record more about each person, import them in bulk, and log removals
changes.body:
Three related changes to how the sign-in allowlist is managed. All of it is
admin-only and goes through the Admin SDK, as the rest of the access control
already does.

## Richer people records

Adds `personalEmail`, `dateOfBirth` and `startDate` to the allowlist entry,
editable in the row editor and included in the CSV export.

The two dates are stored as `YYYY-MM-DD` text rather than Timestamps. A
birthday and a start date have no time and no timezone; as a Timestamp they
land at midnight UTC and read back a day early for anyone west of it — this
office included. Text also sorts chronologically for free and round-trips
through `<input type="date">` unchanged.

The three new fields are deliberately NOT mirrored onto `users/{uid}`, unlike
the name, phones, extension and site. That document is readable by every
signed-in user under firestore.rules, while `allowedUsers` is admin-only, so
mirroring a birthday and a private address would publish them company-wide.
The reasoning is left at each of the four places that could undo it.

Start date is shown on the row ("Started Jan 15, 2024 · 2 years") since it
answers a question people actually ask. Date of birth stays in the editor
rather than on screen every time Settings is opened.

## Spreadsheet import

New Settings → Add People → Spreadsheet, backed by `POST /api/admin/users/import`.
Matches on email, so someone already on the list is updated rather than
duplicated. Two rules shape the implementation, both from this being an admin
tool pointed at the live company directory:

- A blank cell never clears a value. The spreadsheet is a source of updates,
  not a replacement for the record — an admin who fills in the two columns they
  know about must not wipe the phone numbers they left alone. Clearing is done
  in the row editor, where it is unmistakably deliberate.
- A row is applied whole or not at all. An unparseable date rejects the row
  rather than writing it with that one column dropped; a half-applied row looks
  successful and quietly loses data.

The import only adds and updates. It never suspends, never revokes, and reads
nothing into someone's absence from the file, so a directory export that
happens to be missing a person cannot lock them out.

Two-step by design: the panel calls the route once for a plan, shows which rows
would change and which fields on each, and only calls again to apply. There is
no staging copy of this data and no undo, so a preview is not a nicety. Both
passes run identical code over the same file.

Date parsing accepts ISO, US `M/D/YYYY`, and month-name forms, and refuses
two-digit years and day-first slash dates outright — guessing per-cell from
whether the first number exceeds 12 would read two rows of one column in two
different orders, which is how a silent off-by-a-month happens.

Role changes honour the same guards as the role buttons: neither the caller's
own admin role nor a bootstrap admin's can be removed. That column alone is
dropped and explained rather than rejecting the whole row, since the admin's
intent is almost never the one column they may not touch.

Column definitions live in `lib/userImportColumns.ts` and are shared with the
CSV export, so an export can be edited in Excel and uploaded straight back.
`escapeCell`'s formula guard is undone on the way in — a phone number exported
as "+502 …" is written with a leading apostrophe that Excel shows rather than
absorbs, so re-importing our own export would otherwise store it as part of
the number.

`parseCsv`, `headerKey` and `unescapeCell` move into `lib/csv.ts` and the BATS
importer now shares them, so the files this app writes and the files it accepts
back are handled by one implementation. The shared reader also strips a leading
BOM, which `downloadCsv` writes on purpose and which would otherwise glue an
invisible U+FEFF to the first header of our own export.

## Add People replaces Grant Access

"Grant Access" and the import panel were two boxes that both added people, with
nothing to say which one you wanted. They are now one section with a mode
switch, and the typed-in mode takes the whole person rather than just an
address.

That mode adapts to how many addresses are in the box: one and the full detail
form is available, several and the per-person fields grey out, leaving site and
roles — the only two things that can honestly be true of everyone pasted in.
Greyed rather than hidden, so an admin who typed a name and then pasted four
more addresses can see why it stopped applying. The single-address rule is
enforced in the route too, not just the UI.

## Removal log

Revoking access used to erase the entry, the profile and the photo, leaving no
way to answer "who took Ana off the system, and when?". Removals now append to
`removedUsers` first: a copy of the entry plus `removedAt`, `removedBy` and
`removedByUid`.

Written before anything is destroyed, and a failure to write it aborts the
whole removal — an unlogged deletion is the exact gap this closes, so it must
not be reachable by the log write failing.

Generated document ids, not the email. Someone can be added, removed, re-added
and removed again; keying on the address would overwrite the first removal with
the second and destroy the history the log exists to keep.

No `photoPath` is archived: the photo is deleted from Storage as part of the
removal, so the path would only point at a file that is gone.

Retention is permanent, by explicit decision of the business owner
(2026-08-26). The log is the only evidence a person was ever on the system and
the only place their details survive a mistaken removal, so nothing purges,
ages out or trims it, and nothing should be added that does.

The log keeps date of birth and personal email for people who have left, so
`firestore.rules` denies `removedUsers` to the client SDK outright and admins
read it through the guarded `GET /api/admin/users/removed`. Timestamps are
converted to ISO strings at the route — a Firestore Timestamp crosses JSON as a
bare `{_seconds, _nanoseconds}` with no `toDate()`, which every consumer would
otherwise have to know.

Shown collapsed under the people list and fetched only when opened, so a normal
Settings visit does not read a third collection.

## Rules and docs

`firestore.rules` gains an explicit deny for `removedUsers`, matching the
convention `signing_tokens` already uses. Documentary rather than protective —
there is no catch-all match, so the collection was already denied by default —
but it tells the next person to route around it rather than open it up.
Deployed: live rulesets now match this file.

Both handbooks and the schema guide are updated throughout, including the
retention decision and its reasoning.

## Verification

`npm run build` passes. There is no test suite in this repo, so the parsing and
merge logic was exercised separately against in-memory fixtures — date reading,
the blank-cell rule, the export/import column round-trip, the guard behaviour
and the removal-log helpers. Nothing was run against Firestore.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Stop the command-line BATS importer writing the pre-party schema
changes.body:
The August party rebuild (660d057) updated src/lib/batsImport.ts and left
scripts/import-bats.js on the old model. The script still wrote shipperName
from the BATS CustomerName column, set no clientId or consigneeId, and never
populated parties at all. Run against a fresh export it would have written
pre-migration records over all 10,375 imported orders, undoing the migration
before it had been applied.

It also lacked the PRESERVE list, so a refresh would blank the carrier,
driver, uploaded documents and e-signature audit trail on any order that had
them. Nothing was lost in practice: the only order holding that data was
created inside TTMS and has no batsId, so the script's bats-<id> keys could
never reach it. That stops being true once brokers work imported loads.

Ports the script to match batsImport.ts: party registry with shipper and
consignee taken from the Origin and Destination facility segments, PRESERVE,
status reconciliation, and toNameKey suffix canonicalization. Adds --dry-run,
which it was the only writing script to lack.

The duplication cannot be removed - a plain node script cannot import the
TypeScript module, and the script exists because the in-app route is capped
at 60s and cannot finish a full backfill. Both files now carry a keep-in-sync
warning naming this drift, following the accessControl.ts / firestore.rules
convention.

Also ignores *-export-*.csv. The BATS exports are dropped in the project root
by instruction and hold 5,743 client and 11,166 carrier records, with nothing
previously stopping them being committed.

Verified with two dry runs against production: name canonicalization collapsed
Corp./Corporation onto one party, and a run keyed to a real order reported it
as updated rather than new. Neither wrote anything. npm run build passes.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Record who owns the Resend account and what still needs setting up
changes.body:
The handbook flagged the Resend owner as unknown and told the next person
to chase it before handover. There was nobody to chase: the account had
never been created. Signing in at resend.com with Continue with GitHub as
it@totaltransportlogistics.us created it, empty.

The domain is now verified (DKIM and the send subdomain are live in DNS,
Namecheap), so email can be switched on once there is a deployment to
point signing links at. Until then no agreement email has ever been sent.

The in-app Handbook page duplicates this table by hand and carried the
same stale line, so it is corrected too.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Add a read-only check that live rules match the repo
changes.body:
deploy-rules.js --dry-run never contacts the Rules API — it only reports
how many lines it would upload — so it cannot answer whether what is
running in production matches what is committed. That was the gap that
let the rules sit undeployed for five weeks.

compare-rules.js reads the ruleset behind each release and diffs it
against the local file. Read-only: it creates no rulesets and moves no
releases. Exits 1 on drift so it can gate a later CI step.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Stop a second scrollbar appearing under the dashboard shell
changes.body:
Scrolling any dashboard page to the bottom left a tall band of empty
background below the sidebar, reached by a second, outer scrollbar.

The shell itself is not at fault: it is `h-screen overflow-hidden`, exactly
one viewport tall, and the page scrolls inside <main>. Nothing the app
renders sits beside it in <body> either — the tree is AuthProvider wrapping
the shell and nothing else. The height comes from a node the app does not
author: the hidden iframe Firebase Auth appends, the dev overlay, an
extension's injected element. Whatever it is, it stacks under the shell's
100vh and makes the document taller than the viewport.

Chasing the specific node would fix one source and leave the rest, so the
document is pinned instead: `html`/`body` get `height: 100%; overflow: hidden`
while the dashboard is mounted, making a dashboard route incapable of
scrolling the window at all. The class is added by the dashboard layout only
and removed on unmount, so /login and the public /sign/[token] page still
scroll normally.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Show the distance between an order's two addresses
changes.body:
Brokers had no mileage on an order at all, so a lane's length had to be
looked up elsewhere before a rate could be sanity-checked.

The Route section on the new-order form, the edit form and the order
detail page now shows the distance, and an admin picks how it is worked
out in Settings -> Lane Distance:

  Off       nothing is shown, calculated or stored.
  Estimate  free and offline. Default.
  Routes    Google Routes API. Exact road miles, billed per lookup.

Two methods rather than one because the accurate option costs money and
the free one is not accurate enough to bill against. Making that an
explicit, visible choice beats burying either trade-off.

The estimate (src/lib/routeDistance.ts)

  Great-circle distance between the two ZIP centroids, times a circuity
  factor for roads not running straight (1.16-1.22, tapering as the lane
  gets longer, since short hops wander proportionally more on local
  roads). Centroids are the US Census 2023 ZCTA gazetteer, public domain,
  33,791 ZIPs at src/lib/data/zipCentroids.json.

  Measured against ten lanes with known Google driving distances: mean
  absolute error 5.5%, near-zero bias. LA-NYC +2.0%, Chicago-Dallas
  +1.8%, NYC-Miami -1.1%, Seattle-Portland -0.6%. The failure mode is
  systematic and worth knowing: mountain lanes read LOW, because the
  interstate detours a long way around terrain a straight line goes
  through. Denver-Salt Lake is the worst case at -17.5%. Unusually direct
  interstate shots read high (Dallas-Houston +11.7%).

  So: fine for checking a quote or comparing two lanes, NOT for billing
  per mile. Every surface that shows an estimate says so, and laneMilesSource
  records which method produced the number so the two are never confused.

Keeping the Google option from running up a bill

  - The mode is read server-side in /api/route-distance and never taken
    from the request. A client that could name its own method could spend
    money regardless of what Settings says.
  - Distances are looked up once and stored on the order (laneMiles,
    laneMilesSource), not recomputed on read. Under Routes, re-deriving on
