    render would bill on every page view.
  - A suborder inherits the parent's figure: same lane, same answer.
  - The Routes option is greyed out, and the API refuses it, unless
    GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY is set. Nobody can select a mode that silently
    does nothing.
  - The default is Estimate. A default must never be the option that
    spends money.
  - If Routes fails at run time — no key, billing lapsed, an address it
    cannot route — the order falls back to the estimate, records it as an
    estimate, and surfaces Google's own reason so an admin finds out.

The ~800KB centroid table is why the estimate lives behind an API route
rather than running in the browser; the calculation itself is free, so its
debounce is anti-flicker, not rationing.

Also in here, because they touch the same files: docs/handover-guide.md is
renamed to docs/admin-handbook.md and every reference to it updated, at the
owner's request. Mentions of "the handover" as an event, and of the
codebase being "handoverable", are left alone — those describe the act of
handing the system over, not the document.

firestore.rules gains an appSettings block (read for allowed users, writes
Admin SDK only). NOT LIVE: editing the file changes nothing until
`node scripts/deploy-rules.js` is run. Until then brokers will hit
permission errors reading the setting. The dry-run passes.

Verified with npm run build, and the estimator was compiled and run
directly against the lane sample above. Not exercised in the running app:
dev points at production Firebase, and this writes a real settings
document.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Keep the sidebar nav on screen when a page scrolls
changes.body:
The dashboard shell was `min-h-screen`, so on any page taller than the
viewport — a long order list, the Settings page, the Handbook — the shell
grew with its content and the *window* scrolled. The sidebar scrolled with
it and slid off the top, leaving no navigation until you scrolled back up.
`<main>` already had overflow-auto, but it never took effect: its parent
was free to grow, so there was nothing to overflow.

The shell is now exactly the viewport (`h-screen overflow-hidden`) and the
page scrolls inside `<main>` instead. The sidebar stays put.

Within the sidebar, the logo block and the user/sign-out block are pinned
and only the nav list between them scrolls, so the menu still works if it
outgrows the space. Two details worth keeping:

- `min-h-0` on the <nav> is load-bearing. A flex child defaults to
  min-height:auto and refuses to shrink below its content, so without it a
  long list would push the sign-out block off the bottom rather than
  scrolling. Commented in place.
- The nav gets a thin translucent-white scrollbar. The browser default
  renders as a bright grey slab against brand-900 and reads as a rendering
  fault rather than a scrollbar. It only appears once the list overflows —
  with today's eleven items it will not, except on a short window.

Handbook's scrollIntoView calls are unaffected: they resolve against the
nearest scrollable ancestor, which is now <main>.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Fix every maintenance script failing to read a CRLF .env.local
changes.body:
All six scripts in scripts/ parse .env.local with

    line.match(/^([^#=\s][^=]*)=(.*)$/)

JavaScript's `.` does not match a carriage return. On a .env.local saved
with Windows line endings — the normal case on this project's documented
platform — every line ends in \r, no line matches, and every value comes
back undefined.

The failure is loud but misleading. deploy-rules.js dies inside
firebase-admin with

    FirebaseAppError: Service account object must contain a string
    "project_id" property.

which reads as bad credentials rather than a settings file that parsed to
nothing. Confirmed on this machine: .env.local is CRLF, and the dry-run
could not run at all.

That means the rules deploy, the BATS import, the party migration, the
owner resolver and the allowed-users seeder were all non-functional here.
Given this repo's history of rules sitting undeployed for five weeks while
users saw permission errors, a broken deploy script is worth fixing on its
own.

Strips the trailing \r before matching, in all six. Each file is otherwise
untouched; `node --check` passes on all of them, and
`deploy-rules.js --dry-run` now reports both targets as expected.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Capture freight as itemised commodities with dimensions
changes.body:
A load is rarely one uniform object, but an order could only describe a
single commodity with one weight and no dimensions at all. Brokers were
putting sizes in the notes field, where the BOL never picked them up.

Orders now carry a commodities array — one line per item, each with its
own piece count, length/width/height and weight. Units are stored beside
the numbers rather than normalised, so a dimension reads back in the
units it was quoted in.

The existing commodity/pieces/weight fields stay and are derived from the
array on save: order lists, both PDFs, the agreement emails and the
signing page all read them directly. Orders written before this go
through orderCommodityItems(), which collapses the old fields into a
single dimensionless line so every reader can assume an array.

Also adds:

- A conversion calculator beside both order forms. Brokers get sizes
  quoted in metres or feet-and-inches and have to enter one consistent
  set. It is a scratchpad and never writes into the form, so a stray
  keystroke there cannot alter the load that gets booked.

- A Google Maps route link on the order, auto-built from the two
  addresses via the Maps URLs API (no key needed). It stops updating
  itself once a broker types their own — pinning an exact gate or a
  truck-legal route is the reason the field is editable.

The BOL freight table is now one row per item with a dimensions column,
and the agreement routes snapshot a dimensions summary into the signing
token so what a carrier signed against cannot shift afterwards.

Verified with npm run build. Not exercised against the live app: dev
points at production Firebase and creating an order would write a real
one.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Make the carrier and driver fields on an order usable
changes.body:
Three fixes to assigning a carrier, all sharing the same code path:

- The "add a new carrier" action was a trailing dropdown option nobody
  scrolled far enough to see. It is now a button beside the select, with
  the in-list row moved to the top as a second way in.

- Selecting a carrier fills the driver name, phone and licence from that
  carrier's most recent load, since there is no drivers collection to read
  from. Only empty fields, or fields still holding the last guess, are
  touched, and the panel says which order the details came from.

- Contact and driver names are captured as First + Last. They are still
  stored as the single name string the schema has, split on the first
  space, so no backfill of the BATS-imported records is needed.

Carrying a licence forward leaves two orders pointing at one file, so
DriverLicenseUpload now only deletes objects uploaded against the current
order — otherwise removing it here would destroy the older order's copy.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Let brokers add a new carrier without leaving the order
changes.body:
The carrier dropdown only listed carriers that already existed, so booking
a first-time carrier meant navigating to Add Carrier and losing the driver
name, phone and license already entered on the order.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Give the Desktop shortcut the TTMS logo instead of a blank cog
changes.body:
The handbook told admins to build the shortcut with Send to > Desktop, which
leaves it wearing the generic batch-file icon — indistinguishable from any
other .bat on a machine, and unhelpful for the non-technical staff this
launcher exists for.

scripts/ttms.ico is public/logo-circle-nobg.png rendered at 256x256 and wrapped
in an ICO header as a single PNG-compressed entry, which Windows has accepted
since Vista. Committed rather than generated on demand: it is small, it changes
only when the logo does, and requiring a build step would put it out of reach
of the exact person following this chapter.

Step 6 becomes a numbered list ending in Change Icon, and gains a "you should
see" — the other steps in the chapter all confirm they worked, and this one is
the last thing standing between setup and the everyday routine.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Stop the handbook sending new admins to a shortcut that does not exist yet
changes.body:
Chapter 2 opened with "Double-click Start TTMS on the Desktop" — but that
shortcut is created by step 6 of chapter 3. Someone arriving cold at a machine
that has never run TTMS dead-ended on the first line of the everyday routine,
with nothing on the page telling them why.

A caution callout now heads chapter 2 and links to the setup chapter. The
chapters are not reordered: start/stop is read every morning, setup once per
machine, so putting a thirty-minute one-off first would tax the common reader
to help the rare one.

The link needed plumbing. Chapter bodies are module-level data and cannot reach
the page's own jumpTo, so it is passed down by context and used through a new
ChapterLink. A plain #setup anchor was not enough — chapters render collapsed,
so it would have scrolled to a closed header.

Where .env.local comes from
---------------------------
Step 4 said "ask whoever currently runs TTMS for it", which is a dead end
precisely when it matters: that person is away. It now names the IT folder of
the IT & Facilities Google Drive, reached with the usual role account, so a new
admin can serve themselves.

That is deliberately not repeated in docs/handover-guide.md — this page is
admin-gated, that file is readable by anyone who can clone the repo. A comment
at the edit says so, to stop it being helpfully synced across later. Note the
gating is a visibility control, not a secrecy one: the text ships in the client
bundle either way. It is a folder location, never the values.

The "hand this over carefully" callout is rewritten rather than dropped. It
permitted a password manager but forbade "a shared drive", which ruled out
where the file actually lives. It now permits that folder while still ruling
out email, chat and more widely shared drives, and adds a line about checking
sharing settings before copying it anywhere new.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Add an admin-only Handbook page with a clickable index and search
changes.body:
A document an admin has to go and find is a document they do not read. The
operational half of docs/handover-guide.md now lives in the app itself, at
/dashboard/handbook, reachable from the sidebar.

Deliberately only the operational half. The technical reference stays with the
code it describes, where it cannot drift out of step; a card at the foot of the
page points at docs/handover-guide.md, docs/schema-guide.md and CLAUDE.md.

Access
------
The page guards itself, matching Settings: a non-admin who types the URL is
redirected to /dashboard. Filtering the nav list is presentation, not access
control, and Analytics already demonstrates the difference — it is flagged
adminOnly but has no guard, so any signed-in user can still reach it directly.
That is left alone here rather than fixed in passing, but it is a real hole.

Note that this is a visibility control, not a secrecy one: the page's text ships
in the client bundle either way. Nothing on it is secret. The bootstrap admin
addresses it displays are read from BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAILS, which Settings
already pulls into the same bundle, so nothing new is exposed — and reading them
from accessControl.ts rather than copying them means the page cannot go stale
when that list changes.

Chapters as data
----------------
Content is a CHAPTERS array of { id, title, subtitle, body }, not inline
markup. The index and the page body are both generated from it, so a new
section cannot appear in one and be missing from the other.

Index
-----
A Contents dropdown in a sticky toolbar, listing every chapter with its
subtitle. Selecting one expands that chapter before scrolling to it — jumping
to a collapsed heading would otherwise land the reader on nothing. Expand all
and collapse all are available from the same panel.

Search
------
Finds every occurrence, tints them all, marks the current one in a stronger
colour, and scrolls it to the middle of the viewport. Shows "n of m" with
prev/next buttons; Enter and Shift+Enter cycle, Escape clears. Debounced so
it does not rescan on every keystroke.

Two details that matter:

Collapsed chapters stay mounted (hidden, not unmounted) so their text is still
searchable. Any chapter containing a hit is opened before highlighting runs,
because a Range inside a display:none subtree can be neither painted nor
scrolled to.

Highlighting uses the CSS Custom Highlight API, which styles text ranges
without inserting nodes. The usual approach — wrapping matches in <mark> —
means mutating markup React owns and risks stray tags surviving a re-render.
The API is feature-detected through a narrow shim rather than asserting the
globals exist, since it is absent from this TypeScript lib and from older
browsers; where it is missing, the scroll-to-match still works and only the
tint is lost.

The highlight colours are injected at runtime rather than added to globals.css.
Turbopack's CSS parser does not recognise the ::highlight() pseudo-element and
silently drops the rules from the build — the build still succeeds, so the
tint would simply never have appeared in production while looking correct in
development.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Add a handover guide, AI context file, and a double-click launcher
changes.body:
Nothing in this repo explained how to run or take over TTMS. There was no
README, and docs/schema-guide.md covers only the data model. Everything else
lived in one person's head, on a machine that runs the system against live
production Firebase.

docs/handover-guide.md
----------------------
Three parts, because three different people need three different things:

  Part 1  Running TTMS, written for someone who has never opened a terminal.
          Literal click paths, and a "you should see" checkpoint after each
          step so a reader can tell success from failure before continuing.
          Covers the traps that actually stop people: the SmartScreen prompt
          on the .bat, Ctrl+V not working in a terminal, and Windows silently
          saving .env.local as .env.local.txt.

  Part 2  Technical reference. Architecture, the invariants that must not
          break, the maintenance scripts, the data model, and the open
          problems.

  Part 3  Working on TTMS with an AI assistant, including the rules that stop
          one from writing to live production data.

Section 3 documents what was previously undocumented and easy to lose: nearly
every service is reached by signing in with Google as it@ — a role account, so
access survives an individual leaving. It also records that the Claude Code
work was done on a personal, paid account that is not part of the handover.

The guide states plainly, in both Part 1 and Part 2, that there is no
deployment configured (no vercel.json, no CI, no Hosting block) and that local
development therefore reads and writes live company records. That is the
single largest outstanding risk on the project and it is now written down
rather than assumed.

CLAUDE.md
---------
Read automatically by Claude Code on startup. Front-loads the things an
assistant would otherwise get wrong here and could do real damage with:

  - .env.local points at live production; dry-run every script in scripts/
  - security rules do nothing until deploy-rules.js is run
  - BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAILS and canSeeAllParties() are duplicated in
    firestore.rules and must be changed together
  - every API route must guard itself; there is no middleware backstop
  - Broker is derived, never stored — do not add an isBroker field
  - the sign/[token] audit trail is a legal record
  - npm run build is the only automated check that exists

scripts/start-ttms.bat
----------------------
A double-click launcher so non-technical staff never have to use a terminal
for day-to-day operation. Resolves the repo root relative to its own location,
so it works from a Desktop shortcut or wherever the repo is cloned.

Checks for Node and for .env.local before starting, runs npm install when
node_modules is absent, opens the browser once the server has had time to come
up, then runs npm run dev. Every failure path prints what to do next in plain
language instead of a raw error, and pauses so the window does not vanish
before it can be read.

Also corrected here: npm run lint does not work and never has on this repo's
current state. The script still calls `next lint`, removed in Next.js 16, and
there is no eslint.config.js for ESLint 9's flat config. Both documents now say
so, so npm run build is correctly described as the only working check.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Split the name, add a second phone, photos, and CSV export
changes.body:
Follow-on to the directory work, all in the same list.

Names are two fields
firstName and lastName replace the single name box, so the list can be
ordered by either. displayName is still written alongside them as the two
joined: work groups and party approvals read one name off users/{uid} and
have no business splitting it themselves. An entry saved before the split
seeds both inputs from splitName(), which cuts at the LAST space so "Maria
del Carmen Ruiz" keeps Ruiz as the surname rather than guessing at compound
names. No migration — an entry converts the first time it is edited.

Sorting
The four fixed orders became a field plus a direction: first name, last
name, email, work phone, Guatemala phone, extension, date added, each
reversible. Two rules the ordering depends on:

- A blank field is unknown, not empty-string-first, so it sorts last in
  BOTH directions. Pending invites usually have no details at all, and a
  block of blanks at the top of a name sort is noise.
- Email breaks ties, so two people sharing a first name keep a stable order
  instead of whatever the filter pass produced.

Extensions sort as numbers — comparing them as text puts 1050 ahead of 204,
which reads as a bug. The key zero-pads the digits so the same string
compare everything else uses comes out in numeric order. Phone numbers
compare on digits alone, since (555) 123-4567 and 555.123.4567 are the same
number typed twice; the country code is stripped so a number entered with
+1 or +502 files next to the same number entered without it.

Phones
The existing field is the US work number, kept under the `phone` key rather
than renamed to phoneUs — that key is what the profile mirror and everything
reading a single number already point at, and renaming buys only a
migration. phoneGt is new. Both are labelled US/GT in the row, because two
bare numbers side by side give no clue which to dial from where.

Photos
Uploaded from the row editor to avatars/{email}/, shown in place of the
initial. What is stored is the storage PATH, never the download URL: URLs
carry a token and can be regenerated, so a saved one goes stale. Paths
resolve to URLs at render and are cached, because the list re-renders on
every keystroke in the editor.

Photo changes save immediately rather than waiting for the editor's Save —
by then the file is already in Storage, and leaving the record out of step
with the bucket is how orphans happen. Replacing deletes the old object only
after the new path is recorded, so a failed save cannot strand a row on a
file that is already gone. Revoking someone deletes their photo too. The
server refuses any path outside avatars/, since the path is generated
client-side.

CSV export
Exports what is on screen — same filters, same order. Excel is the target,
which drives two things the format does not require: a BOM, without which
Excel decodes in the local codepage and turns Muñoz into MuÃ±oz, and a guard
on cells starting =, +, - or @, which Excel executes as formulas. The guard
prefixes an apostrophe, so a phone typed as "+1 555…" shows one in the
export; that is the accepted cost of not shipping a spreadsheet that runs
whatever a cell says.

CSV rather than xlsx: a real xlsx needs a library, and this needs none.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Turn People With Access into a user directory
changes.body:
Settings listed allowlist entries and little else: no headcount, no way to
narrow the list, no contact details, and no record of when someone was added
or by whom — all of which were already stored on the document.

Summary and filtering
- Count tiles for status (everyone/active/pending/suspended) and permission
  (broker/admin/dispatcher/finance) that double as the filter control for what
  they count. Counts come off the full list, not the filtered one, so the
  numbers hold still while you click around.
- Roles overlap, so the permission tiles can total more than the headcount.
  The summary line says so rather than letting it read as a miscount.
- Sort by name (A-Z, Z-A) or by when the entry was added (newest, oldest).
  Alphabetical uses the display name, falling back to email. Entries with no
  invitedAt sort last in both directions.

Suspension
Removing access was all or nothing: DELETE wipes the entry and its roles, so
taking someone off temporarily meant re-inviting and re-granting from memory.
`suspended` on the allowlist entry blocks sign-in while keeping everything
else, and restoring puts the person back exactly where they were.

It is enforced at four points, all of which were needed: the session route
(403 at sign-in), Firebase Auth (claims cleared, tokens revoked, account
disabled, so a live session ends immediately), the API guards in
firebase-admin, and the Firestore rules. The rules check matters most —
isAllowedUser() tested only that the entry exists, and a suspended entry
still exists. Rules cannot see Auth's `disabled` flag, and an ID token minted
before the suspension stays valid for up to an hour, so without this a
suspended user keeps reading data for the rest of that hour.

Bootstrap admins are exempt, for the same lockout reason they are exempt
everywhere else. Re-pasting a suspended address into Grant Access now returns
"suspended — restore them instead" rather than the false "already has access".

Broker as the default role
What used to render as "No role" is the role most people have: their own
clients and loads, and nothing they do not own. Naming it Broker makes it a
chip you can filter by and click to demote someone back to.

Derived from the absence of the other three rather than stored as isBroker.
A stored flag would permit an account that is neither a broker nor anything
else — a state nothing in the rules enforces, and which would keep full
baseline access anyway.

Sites and contact details
New `sites` collection with a Settings panel: create, rename, delete. Deleting
detaches everyone assigned, clearing siteId from both the allowlist entry and
the profile, because different parts of the app read different copies. Names
are unique, enforced on rename as well as creation.

Users gain displayName, phone, extension and siteId, stored on the entry and
mirrored onto users/{uid} so a change lands without a re-login. A batch invite
carries the roles and the site; names and phone numbers are per-person, so
those are edited from the row afterwards.

An admin-entered name now wins over the one Google reports at sign-in.
Previously Google's won, which would have overwritten the name as soon as the
person next signed in.

firestore.rules is changed but NOT deployed — run scripts/deploy-rules.js.
Until then the suspension gap above is live.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Replace the shipper model with owned parties, roles, and approvals
changes.body:
Clients, shippers and consignees are one `parties` collection. The role lives
on the order (clientId/shipperId/consigneeId), not on the entity, so the same
company can be a shipper on one order and the client on another.

The old model had no way to create a shipper: the new-order form fell back to
a free-text box whenever the shipper list was empty, which stored a name and
no record — so the list stayed empty forever. BATS made it worse by mapping
orders column 8 (CustomerName) onto shipperName, meaning every order's
"shipper" was really its client, and by discarding the facility segment of
Origin/Destination where the real shipper and consignee were held.

Model
- parties collection with per-role tagging and a normalized nameKey, so
  "Acme Corp." and "ACME Corporation" converge. Legal suffixes are
  canonicalized rather than stripped: dropping them would merge "Acme Corp"
  with "Acme Inc", and a wrong merge is far harder to undo than a duplicate.
- Orders carry all three role links plus denormalized name snapshots.
- Clients/Shippers/Consignees are role-filtered views over one detail page.

Ownership
- A party is visible to its owners (users and/or work groups) and to
  admin/dispatch/finance; unowned parties are open to everyone.
- BATS records the owning rep as a name, not an account, so assignedToName
  marks a party owned-but-unclaimed until scripts/resolve-party-owners.js
  maps it to a real user or group.
- Work groups own records on behalf of a team. Membership is mirrored onto
  users/{uid}.groupIds because rules cannot query; both sides are written in
  one transaction.

Approvals
- Using someone else's party needs a per-order, single-use approval.
- The collision check matches on the exact normalized name only and returns
  the owner's name but never the party id, so it cannot be used to enumerate
  records or to attach an unreadable party to an order.
- The approver's IP is read from request headers server-side, and the
  approval snapshot is written to the order with the Admin SDK, so the person
  who benefits from it cannot fabricate it.

Import safety
- The importer preserved nothing, so any re-upload blanked assigned carrier,
  driver, uploaded documents, e-signature audit trails, notes and carrier
  insurance. TMS-owned fields are now kept and BATS supplies the rest.
- Order status reconciles rather than overwrites: the further-along of the
  BATS and TMS statuses wins, so a refresh can advance an order but never
  drag it back. Cancellation is sticky in both directions.

Also fixes Top Clients and the dashboard's Active Clients, which both grouped
on shipperId and so collapsed all revenue into one bucket.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Add a rules deploy script and fix the Settings load-failure state
changes.body:
The rules files in this repo were never deployed — Firestore was running a
ruleset from five weeks earlier that had no `allowedUsers` match, so the
Settings allowlist read hit the default deny and failed. Committing a rules
file does nothing on its own; it has to be uploaded and released.

scripts/deploy-rules.js does that with the admin service account over the
Rules REST API, so it needs no `firebase login` and no CLI install. It uses
firebase-admin cert() for the access token rather than google-auth-library,
which is only a transitive dependency and would break without warning.

The service account can update an existing release but not create one, so a
brand-new bucket or database still needs its first publish from the Console.
The script says so on a 404 instead of surfacing the raw API error.

Settings also rendered "No one has been granted access yet" when the read
failed, which made a permissions problem look like missing data. Track the
failure separately and offer a retry.

changes.author: erwindank
changes.subject: Replace domain-based login with an explicit invite allowlist
changes.body:
Any @totaltransportlogistics.us Google account could previously sign itself
in and auto-create its own profile. Access is now granted per-address: an
admin adds someone under Settings -> Grant Access, which writes an
allowedUsers/{email} document, and that document is what authorizes the
account. Email domain grants nothing on its own.

Enforcement is applied at every layer rather than just the client:

- /api/auth/session verifies the ID token on each sign-in, refuses anyone
  without an allowlist entry, provisions users/{uid} from that entry, and
  mirrors roles into custom claims. AuthContext signs the user out if this
  call fails, so there is no signed-in state without a verified entry.
- Firestore rules gate on a live allowedUsers lookup, so revocation takes
  effect on the next request rather than when the ID token expires.
- users and allowedUsers are closed to client writes, so an uninvited
  account cannot create a profile and nobody can self-promote to admin.
- Storage rules cannot read Firestore, so they gate on the ttlAccess custom
  claim stamped at sign-in. Revoking clears the claim, revokes refresh
  tokens and disables the account; the current ID token stays valid until
  it expires, so Storage lags by at most an hour.
- requireCompanyUser checks the allowlist, and token verification now uses
  checkRevoked so revoked sessions fail immediately.

BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAILS (mirrored by hand in firestore.rules) is always
allowed and always admin so a damaged or empty allowlist cannot lock
everyone out; those accounts cannot be removed or demoted through the UI.
Run scripts/seed-allowed-users.js once when migrating an existing
deployment, otherwise the allowlist starts empty.

Drops the "hd" parameter that pinned the Google account picker to one
domain, since it would block a collaborator an admin deliberately invited
from outside it.

Also fixes three pre-existing Recharts tooltip type errors that were
failing next build; the formatters declared narrower parameters than
Recharts actually passes. Typing only, no change to displayed output.
